docs.title: Kioko
docs.text:
Pluggable, self-managing long-term memory for AI agents, for any framework, any language and any MCP host.

Documentation: https://aion7891.github.io/kioko-docs/ · Install: pip install kioko

The name comes from kioku (記憶), Japanese for "memory": 記 (ki) "to record" and 憶 (oku) "to remember".

Kioko remembers what users tell your agents and hands the right memories back before every reply. That covers who users are, what they prefer, what they are working towards, what they decided, which procedures work and what happened. It manages that memory by itself.

  • Fifteen kinds of memory. Profile, factual, semantic, episodic, working, conversational, goal, procedural, skill, strategy, decision, graph, KV-cache, parametric, and hybrid recall over all of them. Every kind works on every store and every surface.
  • A memory graph that connects them. Every new memory is linked to the memories it relates to, with a type and the evidence: a decision serves a goal, a lesson refines a procedure, a fix resolves an incident. Recall follows the links and tells the agent how things connect. The algorithm is documented in full in graph memory.
  • An intelligence that manages them. It routes each turn into the right kind with the right operation: progress on a goal, a decision that replaces an earlier one, a value that changed, "forget that", a ticket number for this session. It plans which kinds a question needs, and summarises, reflects, pins hot memories and tidies up in the background. It runs offline with rules and algorithms, or with any LLM, where the algorithms gate, validate and fall back.
  • Efficient by design.
    • One model call per turn at most, and none for small talk.
    • Intent-based retrieval within a token budget: about 20% fewer tokens in the measured example.
    • Rolling session summaries.
    • A stable, cacheable prompt prefix that carries the memories needed most.
  • Pluggable everywhere.
    • Stores: in-process, SQLite, Postgres + pgvector, Qdrant, or your own.
    • Embedders, extractors, rankers, processors, summarizers, framework adapters, and each part of the intelligence.
    • Plug in by class, by name, or with a pip-installable entry point.
  • Three ways in, one behaviour.
    • attach() for any Python agent: Agno, LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, OpenAI Agents SDK, AutoGen, smolagents, plain functions.
    • A REST API with OpenAPI for any language or low-code tool.
    • An MCP server for GitHub Copilot, Claude, Cursor and Copilot Studio.
  • No dependencies. The core, SQLite, the offline embedder, the intelligence, the REST/MCP server and the web console use only the Python 3.14 standard library.
  • You can see and steer what it does. Every write, recall and decision is an event. The web console shows them live and lets you manage every user, session and memory. Webhooks push them elsewhere.
 any Python agent ──► attach() / with_memory / MemoryMiddleware ─┐
 any language     ──► REST  /v1   (OpenAPI)                      ├──► MemoryLayer ── 15 kinds of memory
 any MCP host     ──► MCP   /mcp  or stdio                       │      │  intelligence: route · plan · maintain
 other processes  ──► RemoteMemory / connect("http://...")       ┘      └─► store: SQLite · pgvector · Qdrant · yours
                                                                             events ──► console · webhooks

docs.title: Five lines
docs.text:
import kioko

memory = kioko.intelligent("sqlite:///plant-memory.db")      # offline; kioko.intelligent(..., llm=ask) for a model

memory.record_turn("Hi, I'm Asha, a controls engineer at the Pune plant. I prefer short answers.",
                   "Nice to meet you, Asha!", user_id="asha", session_id="mon-shift")
memory.record_turn("My goal is to get line 3 OEE above 85% by December 31.",
                   "Noted - let's track it.", user_id="asha", session_id="mon-shift")
memory.record_turn("To reset the safety relay, switch off the main breaker, then press reset for 5 seconds, "
                   "then switch the breaker back on.", "Thanks, saved.", user_id="asha", session_id="mon-shift")

print(memory.recall("The safety relay tripped again - what do I do?", user_id="asha", session_id="tue-shift"))

<memory>
Long-term memory about the user. Use it to personalise your answer. ...

Instructions from the user:
- User prefers short answers.

About the user:
- User is a controls engineer.
- User works at the Pune plant.
- User's name is Asha.

The user's open goals:
- Get line 3 OEE above 85% by December 31 (medium, 0%, due 2026-12-31)

Procedures that may apply:
- reset the safety relay: 1) Switch off the main breaker; 2) Press reset for 5 seconds; 3) Switch the breaker back on
</memory>

Each sentence went to the kind where it belongs:

  • name, role and employer became profile slots;
  • the answer-style preference became a standing instruction;
  • the goal became a goal with a due date;
  • the how-to became a procedure.

The next day's question was recognised as a how-to. No model was called. The guide continues from here, through the agent loop, frameworks, stores, the service, MCP, the console and production.

Try it without writing code:

kioko demo                                  # scripted conversation in the terminal
kioko ui --db memory.db --intelligence      # web console at http://localhost:8765 (also serves /v1 and /mcp)

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Requires Python 3.14 or newer. On Windows, run the commands below through the launcher: py -3.14 -m ....

pip install kioko                 # the core: no third-party dependencies
pip install "kioko[pgvector]"     # + Postgres / pgvector (psycopg)
pip install "kioko[agno]"         # + the Agno adapter
pip install .                     # or from the source folder

Name. The package is kioko on PyPI. The standard romanization kioku is taken there by an unrelated cache library, and kioku-lite, kioku-agent-kit and kioku-mcp are other agent-memory projects. kioko keeps the meaning and stays distinct.

docs.title: attach(): any agent, one line
docs.text:
from kioko import MemoryLayer, attach

memory = MemoryLayer.sqlite("memory.db")    # or kioko.intelligent("sqlite:///memory.db") to let it manage itself

# LangChain runnable or LangGraph graph: user and thread come from the config
chain = attach(prompt | llm, memory)
chain.invoke({"input": "I prefer short answers"},
             config={"configurable": {"user_id": "kumar", "thread_id": "t1"}})

# Agno agent: hooks + memory tools
agent = attach(Agent(model=OpenAIChat(id="gpt-4o-mini")), memory)
agent.run("What do you know about me?", user_id="kumar")

# CrewAI crew: say which input holds the user's text
crew = attach(my_crew, memory, input_key="topic", user_id="kumar")

# OpenAI Agents SDK, or anything else: wrap the call in a function
from agents import Agent, Runner
support = Agent(name="Support", instructions="You are a helpful assistant.")
ask = attach(lambda message: Runner.run_sync(support, message).final_output, memory)
ask("I prefer metric units", user_id="kumar")

attach(target, memory=None, *, adapter=None, **options) picks the first adapter whose matches() accepts the target, and returns what to use from now on (usually the same object):

Adapter Targets What it does agno Agno Agent / Team Pre-hook recalls memories into the input, post-hook learns, plus save/search/update/delete_memory tools scoped to run_context.user_id. method Any object with invoke/ainvoke, stream/astream, run/arun, chat/achat, ask/aask, query/aquery, kickoff/kickoff_async: LangChain runnables, LangGraph graphs, CrewAI crews, your classes Wraps those methods in place (same object, same type). Objects that refuse new attributes get a MemoryProxy. methods=[...] picks the methods. callable Functions and callable objects, sync, async or streaming Returns a wrapped function (with_memory). yours Anything Registered adapters and installed plug-ins are tried first (see Extend).

What is injected, and where. The memory block goes where the agent will read it, keeping the input's shape:

Input shape Where the memory block goes a string in front of the text a message list (OpenAI dicts, LangChain messages, ("human", "hi") tuples) a system message after your own system messages a dict with messages (LangGraph state, chat-completion requests) the same, inside messages a dict with input/query/question/prompt/message/... in front of that field (input_key= picks another field) a pydantic model or dataclass with such a field (LangChain prompt values too) on a copy one message with multi-part content (vision) a leading text part

Who is talking. The user and session ids come from user_id= / session_id= / thread_id= arguments (removed before the call unless the target declares them), then a LangChain/LangGraph config={"configurable": {...}} (or config["metadata"]), then the payload dict itself. Without one, user_id= and session_id= given to attach() are the defaults. scope=lambda args, kwargs: ... decides first; it receives the call's original arguments, and if it returns None the rules above apply.

Replies. Replies are read from strings, {"output"|"answer"|"content": ...}, LangGraph state (the last assistant message), LangChain messages, Agno RunOutput, OpenAI Agents RunResult.final_output and CrewAI CrewOutput.raw. Streams (generators and async generators) pass through untouched and are recorded when they finish.

Nested calls. When a wrapped method calls another wrapped method of the same object (chat() → run(), or stream() → invoke(), even through a thread pool), memory is added once and the turn is recorded once. Async streams fetch memory off the event loop. If a stream fails, the agent's own error is raised, never a recording error.

detach(agent) undoes attach() and restores the original methods. Calling attach() again replaces the previous wrapping, so the newest options win. Attach once at startup and pass user_id with each call; don't re-attach per request. attach(agent, "http://memory:8765"), or attach(agent) with KIOKO_URL set, connects to a shared service instead of a local layer.

Checkpointed threads. For LangChain and LangGraph targets the injected system message carries a stable id (kioko-memory), so a checkpointed LangGraph thread replaces last turn's memory message instead of piling up a new one each turn. Memory blocks are never stored as history or learned from, even when they come back inside a later input.

docs.title: Agno in detail
docs.text:
from kioko.integrations import AgnoMemory

mem = AgnoMemory(memory, inject="input", background=False)   # what attach() uses for Agno agents
agent = Agent(model=..., tools=mem.tools(), pre_hooks=[mem.pre_hook], post_hooks=[mem.post_hook])
Piece What it does pre_hook Retrieves the user's instructions, profile facts and the memories relevant to the message, and puts the memory block in front of run_input.input_content. post_hook Stores the exchange as session history, extracts and writes new memories, then restores the original input in the stored run, so memory blocks don't pile up in Agno's history. tools save_memory, search_memory, update_memory, delete_memory. They declare run_context, so Agno injects the current run (hidden from the model) and the tools act on run_context.user_id.

Options: agent_id, inject="input" | "none", learn, tools, allow_update, allow_delete, context_limit, background (learn in a worker thread), restore_input. Also: LLMExtractor(llm=agno_agent), AgnoEmbedder(any_agno_embedder), and export_to_agno / import_from_agno to sync with Agno's built-in user memories. The adapter follows Agno's documented 3.x API (2.2.7+). Run python -m unittest tests.test_agno_contract -v once with Agno installed to check it against the real package.

docs.title: Lower-level building blocks
docs.text:
from kioko import MemoryMiddleware, with_memory

@with_memory(memory)                                     # sync, async or streaming functions
def my_agent(message: str, memory_context: str = "") -> str:
    return call_llm(system=memory_context, user=message)

hooks = MemoryMiddleware(memory, agent_id="support-bot")  # inside a graph node, a task, your own loop
ctx = hooks.before(question, user_id="kumar", session_id="s1")   # str(ctx) is the prompt block
reply = run_my_agent(question, context=str(ctx))
hooks.after(question, reply, user_id="kumar", session_id="s1")   # history + learning

tools = memory.tools(user_id="kumar")                    # OpenAI / Azure OpenAI function calling
messages = memory.inject([{"role": "user", "content": question}], user_id="kumar")
response = client.chat.completions.create(model="gpt-4o-mini", messages=messages,
                                          tools=tools.openai_schemas())
for call in response.choices[0].message.tool_calls or []:
    output = tools.call(call.function.name, call.function.arguments)

tools.functions() returns plain functions with type hints and docstrings, ready to register as tools in LangChain (StructuredTool.from_function), CrewAI, smolagents, AutoGen or the OpenAI Agents SDK (function_tool). The tools only read and change the memories of the user they are bound to.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: Concept Details Memory types fact, preference, episodic, instruction, summary, semantic, goal, procedure, skill, strategy, decision, working, entity, relation, parametric (and index for the layer's own bookkeeping). Each has a typed manager; see memory types. Any other string works too. Scope user_id and an optional agent_id. agent_id=None shares a user's memories across agents. session_id records where a memory came from; search never filters by it. Without a session_id, each user gets their own default:<user_id> session, so users never share history. Slot keys e.g. profile.location, opinion:hiking. Writing a new value to the same key updates the memory and keeps the old value in metadata["history"]. Resolution Similarity compares only against memories without a slot key, so a keyed write never merges into a different slot. Cosine ≥ dedup_threshold (0.9) reinforces the existing memory, and cosine ≥ contradiction_threshold (0.8) with opposite polarity supersedes it. ttl_seconds follows the latest write. Context memory.context(query, user_id=...) / memory.recall(...) return up to fifteen sections: instructions, profile, goals and pinned memories (the stable, cacheable part), the session's working memory, relevant facts and episodes, knowledge, graph relations, procedures, skills, lessons, decisions, how these memories connect (links), the session summary and recent turns. budget_tokens= keeps the most important items that fit. str(ctx) is the prompt block. Short-term memory record_turn, add_message, get_history, summarize_session (writes one summary memory per session). Ranking HybridRanker scores vector similarity, keyword (IDF-weighted term coverage), recency (half-life decay) and importance. Results carry the per-signal breakdown. Events memory.subscribe(callback) receives memory.added/updated/deduplicated/dropped/deleted/searched/extracted/managed/pinned/unpinned/consolidated, context.built, session.summarized and history.appended. Stores that support it persist them, which is what the console and /v1/events read. Async aadd, asearch, acontext, abuild_context, alearn, arecord_turn, arecall, aconsolidate, amanage, amaintain.

docs.title: The console: see and manage memory in the browser
docs.text:
The console is a web UI over any Kioko memory. In it you can:

  • chat with an agent and watch each turn's recall, prompt injection and learning;
  • browse, search, edit, pin and delete memories;
  • inspect every memory kind, the knowledge graph and the session scratchpads;
  • preview what the intelligence would do with a message;
  • plan and run a recall within a token budget;
  • follow everything live.

It is part of the package (standard library only) and also serves the REST API (/v1) and MCP (/mcp).

docs.title: Open it
docs.text:
pip install kioko-0.6.0-py3-none-any.whl
kioko ui --open                                   # ./kioko.db, http://127.0.0.1:8765

Point it at the memory you want to look at:

You want to look at Command a SQLite file kioko ui --db path/to/memory.db Postgres + pgvector kioko ui --store "postgresql://kioko:<password>@db:5432/kioko" (or KIOKO_PG_DSN) Qdrant kioko ui --store qdrant://localhost:6333/kioko_memories a JSON config (MemoryLayer.from_config) kioko ui --config kioko.json a running Kioko service kioko ui --url http://memory-service:8765 (API key from KIOKO_API_KEY) ... with the self-managing intelligence on add --intelligence, or --intelligence-llm my_app.models:ask ... chatting with your own agent add --agent my_agent:build (build(memory) returns agent(message, *, user_id, session_id)) on another port add --port 8800

From Python, for example from a notebook:

from kioko import intelligent
from kioko.ui import serve

memory = intelligent("sqlite:///memory.db")
serve(memory, port=8765, open_browser=True)             # blocks; Ctrl+C to stop

With --url, the console manages a running service. Every view, edit and maintenance action goes through the service's REST API, so you can inspect the memory of a deployed agent fleet from your laptop. Intelligence previews then run on the service, with its configuration.

docs.title: Manage and check sessions
docs.text:
The left sidebar lists the users in the store and the selected user's sessions, with message counts. Click a session to make it the current one, or + to start a new one. The current session is the one the Playground chats in, whose working memory and summary the Kinds and Recall tabs show, and which End this session wraps up.

  • Playground. Chat as the selected user in the selected session. Under every reply, the inspector shows the turn's pipeline:
    • Recall: what was retrieved, with score breakdowns;
    • Inject: the exact memory block the agent received;
    • Learn: what was written, or, with intelligence on, the decisions with their reasons (goal.progress, decision.supersede, working.set ...).

Run guided demo walks through it all. * Memories. Every memory of the user: type, slot key, importance, source, how often it was recalled, previous values, and pinned status. You can: * search with hybrid scoring and per-signal bars; * add, edit (the old value is kept), delete, and Pin / Unpin; * try the extractor on a message as a dry run. * Kinds. One card per memory kind with its count. Open one to manage it: * profile slots, facts, knowledge (yours and shared); * the episode timeline, the session's working memory and conversation summary; * goals with progress bars, procedures with their track record, skills, lessons and the decision log with supersession; * the KV-cache prefix and cache statistics, and the fine-tuned models.

Preview consolidation and Consolidate now run the maintenance pass. * Intelligence. * Process a turn: type what the user said (and optionally the reply), click Preview decisions to see every operation the intelligence would apply, with reasons and importance, then Apply. The example chips cover the common cases. * Plan a recall: shows the intents of a question, the sections it needs and their caps, and runs the recall with that plan. * Maintenance: Reflect, Pin hot memories, Consolidate and End this session. * Pinned memories: what is always in context, with Unpin. * The header shows whether the memory manages itself, in which mode, and the counters: turns managed, turns skipped by the gate, model calls, fallbacks, and operations by type. * Graph. Two views: * Memory graph: the user's memories as nodes (coloured by kind) and the links between them as edges (dashed: structure such as a sub-goal or a replaced decision; green: a fix that worked). Click a memory to see each link with its evidence, weight and author, Unlink it, see what lies further away (with the chain of links), or Centre on this memory. Link unlinked memories links what was written before linking was on. * Entity graph: the knowledge graph as a picture, centred on an entity and limited to a depth, with every relation and its history. * Recall. The block an agent would receive for a question: * set a token budget, the retrieval mode (hybrid RRF or ranker) and the plan (by intent, or every kind); * see the tokens used, the sections, why each memory was recalled (signals and score - linked when a memory came in through its links), the connections among them, and what the budget left out. * Activity. A live feed of everything the memory did: writes, recalls, extraction, history and, under Intelligence, managed turns, pins and consolidation. It includes agents in other processes that share the database. Tick All users to see everyone. * Integrate. This server's live REST and MCP endpoints and ready-to-copy snippets (Python, REST, MCP, extending), filled in with this server's URL and the selected user.

docs.title: Reach a console on a server
docs.text:
The console has no login. Keep it on a machine you control, and reach it through a tunnel instead of opening a port:

# on the server
kioko ui --db /data/memory.db                    # binds to 127.0.0.1:8765
# on your laptop
ssh -N -L 8765:127.0.0.1:8765 you@server         # then open http://localhost:8765

Even better, leave the server running kioko serve (with an API key) and run the console locally against it: kioko ui --url https://memory.example.com with KIOKO_API_KEY set.

In Docker, map the port to loopback only:

docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:8765:8765 -v kioko-data:/data kioko \
  kioko ui --host 0.0.0.0 --db /data/memory.db --intelligence

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• The console binds to 127.0.0.1 by default. It prints a warning when bound anywhere else, because its pages and /api have no authentication.
  • KIOKO_API_KEY protects /v1 and /mcp on the same server, not the console pages.
  • It checks the Host header (against DNS rebinding) and the Origin header (against cross-site requests), never accepts cross-origin calls to /api, and serves a strict Content-Security-Policy.
  • Anyone who can open the console can read and change every user's memories. Use kioko serve for anything shared, and the console as an operator's tool.

docs.title: 01 Profile memory
docs.text:
Who the user is - one value per slot, older values kept as history.

examples/cookbook/01_profile.py

from kioko import MemoryLayer

memory = MemoryLayer()
user = "kumar"

memory.profile.set("name", "Kumar Nishant", user_id=user)
memory.profile.set("role", "senior AI engineer", user_id=user)
memory.profile.set("employer", "Rockwell Automation", user_id=user)
memory.profile.set("location", "Pune", user_id=user)
memory.profile.set("location", "Bengaluru", user_id=user)    # moved: the slot is updated, not duplicated

print(memory.profile.get(user_id=user))
print("location history:", [h["content"] for h in memory.profile.history("location", user_id=user)])
print(memory.profile.render(user_id=user))

# Conversations fill the same slots automatically
memory.learn("By the way, I'm now based in Hyderabad.", user_id=user)
print("after learn():", memory.profile.get("location", user_id=user))

Output:

{'employer': 'Rockwell Automation', 'location': 'Bengaluru', 'name': 'Kumar Nishant', 'role': 'senior AI engineer'}
location history: ['User lives in Pune.']
- User works at Rockwell Automation.
- User lives in Bengaluru.
- User's name is Kumar Nishant.
- User is a senior AI engineer.
after learn(): Hyderabad

docs.title: 02 Factual memory
docs.text:
Facts and preferences, with confidence and verification.

examples/cookbook/02_facts.py

from kioko import MemoryLayer

memory = MemoryLayer()
user = "kumar"

memory.facts.add("The Pune plant runs ControlLogix 5580 controllers", user_id=user, confidence=0.7,
                 topics=["plant"])
memory.facts.add("User prefers answers with code first", user_id=user, preference=True)
manager = memory.facts.add("User's manager is Krutika", user_id=user, key="work.manager")

memory.facts.verify(manager, user_id=user, confidence=0.99)           # confirmed by the user / a system of record

from kioko import MemoryLayer

def llm(system: str, user: str) -> str:
    """Stand-in for a chat model: it just shows what the model would receive."""
    lines = [line for line in system.splitlines() if line.startswith("- ")]
    return f"(model saw {len(lines)} memory lines) " + (lines[0][2:] if lines else "Nice to meet you!")

    memory.record_turn(message, reply, user_id=user_id, session_id=session_id)                 # 3. learn

docs.text:
Kioko.intelligent() decides what each turn means for memory - which kind it belongs to and which operation to apply - plans what to retrieve per question, and tidies up on its own. Offline (rules + algorithms); pass llm= to let a model decide (see 21_llm_intelligence.py).

import kioko

memory = kioko.intelligent()          # or kioko.intelligent("sqlite:///memory.db"), "postgresql://...", ...
user, session = "kumar", "shift-1"

# 1. Preview what the intelligence would do with a message - nothing is written in a dry run.
preview = memory.manage("I'm Kumar, I live in Pune. My goal is to stabilise line 3 by November 30.",
                        user_id=user, dry_run=True)
print(preview.summary())

# 2. A real conversation. In an agent, this is the record_turn() you already call after each reply.
turns = [
    "I'm Kumar, I live in Pune. My goal is to stabilise line 3 by November 30.",
    "We decided to use Qdrant for the maintenance notes because it is fast.",
    "I'm debugging ticket INC-4521, the drive shows error E-217 on line 3.",
    "To reset the safety relay, switch off the breaker, then press reset for 5 seconds, then switch it back on.",
    "We switched from Qdrant to pgvector because we already run Postgres.",
    "I'm about 60% done with stabilising line 3.",
    "thanks!",
]
for text in turns:
    report = memory.manage(text, user_id=user, session_id=session)
    print(f"\nyou > {text}")
    for line in report.summary().splitlines():
        print("      " + line)

# 3. Every kind was updated where it belongs.
goal = memory.goals.active(user_id=user)[0]
print("\ngoal:", goal.line())
print("decision:", [(d.title, d.chosen, d.status) for d in memory.decisions.log(user_id=user)])
print("working memory:", memory.working(session, user_id=user).snapshot())

# 4. Retrieval is planned by intent: a how-to question gets the procedure first; small talk costs nothing.
ctx = memory.recall("How do I reset the safety relay?", user_id=user, session_id=session)
print("\nplan:", ctx.plan["intents"], "-", ctx.plan["reason"])
print(ctx.text)

# 5. Feedback closes the loop: "that worked" is credited to the procedure the agent just used.
memory.record_turn("How do I reset the safety relay?", "Switch off the breaker, press reset, switch it on.",
                   user_id=user, session_id=session)
memory.recall("That worked, thanks!", user_id=user, session_id=session)
memory.record_turn("That worked, thanks!", "Great!", user_id=user, session_id=session)
procedure = memory.procedures.get("reset the safety relay", user_id=user)
print("procedure track record:", procedure.successes, "success,", procedure.failures, "failures")

memory.working(session, user_id=user).set("root_cause", "a loose encoder cable")
print("\nend of session:", memory.end_session(session, user_id=user)["result"])
print("intelligence stats:", {k: v for k, v in memory.intelligence.stats().items() if k in ("turns", "gated")})

docs.title: 21 Model-driven memory management
docs.text:
One LLM call per turn decides every memory operation, and Kioko's algorithms skip trivial turns (no call), validate what the model proposes, and take over if the model fails.

Any prompt -> text function works. With OpenAI / Azure OpenAI it is a few lines:

from openai import OpenAI                       # or AzureOpenAI(azure_endpoint=..., api_version=...)
client = OpenAI()

def ask(prompt: str) -> str:
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(model=os.environ["KIOKO_MODEL"], temperature=0,
                                           response_format={"type": "json_object"},
                                           messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return reply.choices[0].message.content

memory = kioko.intelligent("sqlite:///memory.db", llm=ask)

An Agno agent (llm=Agent(model=...)) or a LangChain chat model works the same way. This recipe uses a scripted stand-in model so it runs offline and prints the same thing every time.

examples/cookbook/21_llm_intelligence.py

import json

import kioko

SCRIPT = {   # what our stand-in "model" answers for each user message
    "I'm Kumar from the Pune plant. Our team wants to cut unplanned downtime on line 3 by 20% this year.": [
        {"op": "profile.set", "slot": "location", "value": "Pune", "reason": "where the user works"},
        {"op": "goal.add", "title": "Cut unplanned downtime on line 3 by 20%", "due": "2026-12-31",
         "priority": "high", "reason": "a team objective with a target"}],
    "After a long debate we picked Grafana over Power BI for the line dashboards, mostly for the alerting.": [
        {"op": "decision.add", "title": "Dashboard tool for line 3", "chosen": "Grafana",
         "options": ["Grafana", "Power BI"], "rationale": "better alerting", "reason": "a decision with a reason"}],
    "Downtime is already down 12%.": [
        {"op": "goal.progress", "target": "g1", "progress": 0.6, "note": "12% of the 20% target",
         "reason": "12 of 20 percentage points"}],
    "My API key is sk-EXAMPLE-not-a-real-key-000, keep it for later.": [
        {"op": "fact.add", "content": "User's API key is sk-EXAMPLE-not-a-real-key-000"}],
}
FAILS_ON = "I prefer bullet points over long paragraphs."   # the stand-in model "fails" on this one


def stand_in_model(prompt: str) -> str:
    """Pretends to be an LLM: finds the user's message in the prompt and answers with scripted JSON."""
    said = prompt.rsplit("Conversation:", 1)[1].split("user: ", 1)[1].split("\n", 1)[0].strip()
    if said == FAILS_ON:
        return "Sorry, I can't produce JSON right now."          # a failing model: the offline router takes over
    return json.dumps({"operations": SCRIPT.get(said, [])})


calls = []
memory = kioko.intelligent(llm=lambda prompt: calls.append(prompt) or stand_in_model(prompt))
user = "kumar"

for text in [*SCRIPT, "thanks!", FAILS_ON]:
    report = memory.manage(text, user_id=user)
    print(f"\nyou > {text}\n      [{report.router}, {report.llm_calls} LLM call(s)]")
    for op in report.ops:
        note = "" if op.status == "applied" else f"   <- {op.status}: {op.error}"
        print(f"      {op.describe()}{note}")
    if report.gated:
        print(f"      skipped before calling the model: {report.gated}")
    if report.fallback:
        print(f"      the model failed ({report.fallback}); the offline router decided instead")

print("\nwhat the model was shown for 'Downtime is already down 12%.':")
prompt = next(p for p in calls if "Downtime is already down 12%." in p)
print("\n".join("   " + line for line in prompt.split("Open goals:")[1].split("Current decisions:")[0].strip().splitlines()))
print("\ngoal now:", memory.goals.active(user_id=user)[0].line())
print("model calls:", len(calls), "for", memory.intelligence.stats()["turns"], "turns")

docs.text:
Tokens per recall with and without a plan, model calls skipped by the gate, and what rides in the cacheable prefix. Runs offline; the numbers are measured, not assumed.

examples/cookbook/22_efficiency.py

import json
import math

import kioko
from kioko import FunctionEmbedder, HashingEmbedder

# A stand-in for a semantic embedding model. Like real ones, it gives unrelated texts a baseline similarity, so
# every memory competes for a place in the context - the situation in which the plan's caps matter. (With the
# default lexical embedder retrieval is already narrow and planning mostly changes *what* is retrieved.)
_lexical = HashingEmbedder()


def semantic_like(text):
    vector = [0.8 * x for x in _lexical.embed_one(text)]
    vector[0] += 0.6
    norm = math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in vector))
    return [x / norm for x in vector]


memory = kioko.intelligent(embedder=FunctionEmbedder(semantic_like, batch=False))
user = "kumar"

# -- a realistic memory: profile, rules, goals, decisions, procedures, lessons, facts, episodes, knowledge ---------
memory.profile.set("name", "Kumar", user_id=user)
memory.profile.set("location", "Pune", user_id=user)
memory.profile.set("role", "senior AI engineer", user_id=user)
memory.procedures.add_rule("Always cite the ticket number", user_id=user)
memory.goals.add("Stabilise line 3", user_id=user, priority="high", due="2026-11-30")
memory.goals.add("Pass the Azure AI Engineer exam", user_id=user, due="2027-03-31")

                    ("Restart the OPC UA server", ["Stop the service", "Clear the cache", "Start the service"]),
                    ("Recalibrate the line 3 encoder", ["Stop the line", "Run the wizard", "Verify 10 cycles"]),
                    ("Deploy the agent", ["Run the tests", "Build the image", "Roll out to staging"])]:
    memory.procedures.add(name, steps=steps, user_id=user)

memory.strategies.reflect("debugging drives", "replace the drive", "failure", user_id=user,

               f"device with firmware {i % 5}.{i % 3}", user_id=user)

docs.title: 23 Memory graph
docs.text:
Every memory is linked to the memories it relates to - a decision serves a goal, a fix resolves an incident, a lesson refines a procedure - with the evidence for each link. Recall follows the links and tells the agent how things connect. The algorithm is described in docs/graph-memory.md.

examples/cookbook/23_memory_graph.py

import kioko

memory = kioko.intelligent()          # linking is on with the intelligence (or MemoryLayer(auto_link=True))
user = "kumar"

# 1. A goal, and one fact in the entity graph: Kioko uses pgvector.
goal = memory.goals.add("Ship the Kioko memory layer by December 15", user_id=user)
memory.graph.add("Kioko", "uses", "pgvector", user_id=user)

# 2. A decision mentions pgvector, not Kioko - the entity graph bridges them.
report = memory.manage("We decided to use pgvector because we already run Postgres.", user_id=user)
print(report.summary())

# 3. An incident: a fault, then its fix, in one session. Neither says "resolves"; the algorithm sees a problem and
#    a fix about the same asset in the same session.
memory.procedures.add("Clear a conveyor jam on line 3", user_id=user,
                      steps=["Press stop", "Open the guard", "Remove the jammed bottle", "Reset the drive"])
for text in ("The line 3 conveyor jammed twice this morning.", "Line 3 keeps faulting with error E-217.",
             "Found it: the encoder cable on line 3 was loose."):
    memory.manage(text, user_id=user, session_id="shift-1")
memory.strategies.reflect("clearing conveyor jams", "reset the drive before reopening the guard", "success",
                          lesson="always check the photo-eye alignment after a jam", user_id=user)

# 4. Every link carries its type, weight, author and evidence.
print("\nlinks of the goal:")
for link in memory.graph.links(goal.id):
    print(f"  {link.line()}  [{link.weight:.2f} {link.by}]  {link.why}")
fault = next(r for r in memory.list(user_id=user, memory_types=["episodic"]) if "E-217" in r.content)
print("\nlinks of the fault:")
for link in memory.graph.links(fault.id):
    print(f"  {link.line()}  [{link.weight:.2f} {link.by}]  {link.why}")

# 5. Why are two memories (not) linked? explain() shows the evidence the algorithm used.
tea = memory.add("User likes green tea.", user_id=user)
verdict = memory.graph.explain(tea.id, fault.id)
print("\ntea vs fault:", verdict.linked, {k: round(v, 2) for k, v in verdict.signals.items() if v})

# 6. Spreading activation: what is connected to the lesson, best first, and through which links.
lesson = memory.strategies.list(user_id=user)[0]
print("\nrelated to the lesson:")
for item in memory.graph.related(lesson.id, depth=2, limit=4):
    print(f"  {item.score:.2f}  {item.record.content[:60]}")
    for step in item.path:
        print(f"        via {step.line()}")

# 7. Recall follows the links and says how the memories connect.
ctx = memory.recall("Line 3 is faulting with E-217 again - what do we know?", user_id=user)
print()
print(ctx.text)
print("brought in by links:", [r.record.content[:40] for section in ("procedures", "strategies", "relevant")
                               for r in getattr(ctx, section) if "linked" in r.signals])

# 8. Link by hand (never fades), trace a chain, and draw the graph.
link = memory.graph.link(lesson.id, fault.id, type="learned_from", why="the E-217 night taught us this")
print("\nmanual:", link.line(), link.by)
print("trace lesson -> fault:", " | ".join(step.line() for step in memory.graph.trace(lesson.id, fault.id)))
graph = memory.graph.memories(user_id=user)
print("graph:", graph["stats"])

# 9. Memories written before linking was on are linked in one call.
legacy = kioko.MemoryLayer(auto_link=False)
legacy.add("The OPC UA server on the HMI panel rejected our client certificate.", user_id=user,
           memory_type="episodic")
legacy.strategies.reflect("debugging OPC UA", "restart the server", "failure",
                          lesson="check the OPC UA certificate trust list first", user_id=user)
print("\nconnect():", {k: v for k, v in legacy.graph.connect(user_id=user).items() if k != "duration_ms"})

From the source repository

The Docker and compose files named here are in the source repository, which is not public. Any image that runs pip install kioko and kioko serve works the same way.
