docs.title: Production notes
docs.text:
• Embeddings. The default HashingEmbedder is lexical: it matches words, word pairs and character trigrams, not meaning, so "car" and "automobile" don't match. Use OpenAIEmbedder, AzureOpenAIEmbedder, AgnoEmbedder or FunctionEmbedder for semantic recall. After you change embedders, run memory.reembed() once. Tune HybridRanker(min_vector_only=...) to your embedder's cosine range.
  • Extraction and management. The offline rules and intelligence cover common English phrasings: identity, location, work, likes and dislikes, instructions, goals and progress, decisions and changes, procedures, lessons, dated events, "remember ..." and "forget ...". For open-ended conversations and other languages, give the intelligence a model (kioko.intelligent(llm=...)); the rules stay as gate and fallback.
  • Scale. Without vector_search, search scores every memory in the user's scope: about 5–30 ms for a few hundred memories, ~150 ms for 1,000. Past that, use the pgvector or Qdrant store. The service is a threaded standard-library server, which is enough for an internal agent fleet. For heavy traffic, run several instances behind a load balancer on Postgres, and lower context_cache_ttl.
  • Secrets and PII. DropSecrets is on by default (passwords, API keys, tokens, private keys, card numbers). Add RedactPII to mask e-mails and phone numbers. Processors run on every write and every update, through any channel (Python, REST, MCP, tools, console).
  • Languages. Storage, tokenization, the offline embedder and search work in any script, and tool and MCP output keeps non-ASCII text readable. The rule-based extraction only understands English, so use a model (LLMExtractor, or the intelligence with llm=) for other languages.
  • Python 3.14 annotations. Annotations are evaluated lazily in 3.14 (PEP 649), so an agent function may annotate with a class defined later in the module. attach() / with_memory never force that evaluation: they read signatures with annotationlib.Format.FORWARDREF and copy the lazy __annotate__ function.
  • Concurrency. SQLite runs in WAL mode with one serialized connection per process. That's fine for a service plus the console. For many writers, use Postgres + pgvector.

docs.title: Extend it
Graph memory: how Kioko connects memories
docs.text:
Kioko's graph memory has two layers:

Layer What it holds Example Where Entity graph Who and what is related to what: triples with temporal validity (Kumar) -reports_to-> (Krutika), (Kioko) -uses-> (pgvector) memory.graph.add(), relations(), neighbors(), path() (memory types) Memory links Which memories belong together, and how decision "use pgvector" serves goal "Ship Kioko by Dec 15"; event "found a loose encoder cable" resolves event "line 3 faults with E-217" memory.graph.link(), links(), related(), trace(), explain(), connect(), memories()

This document is about the second layer: the algorithm that links every new memory to the memories it is related to, and the way recall reads those links back. The entity graph feeds into it as one source of evidence ("Kioko uses pgvector" connects a decision about pgvector to a goal about Kioko).

Why bother? Similarity search finds memories that look like the question. Many useful memories don't: the decision that a goal depends on, the fix that solved last month's incident, the lesson learned from a failure. Links capture those relationships when the memory is written, while the context is fresh, and recall can then follow them.

Contents:

  1. Quick start
  2. What a link is
  3. The linking algorithm (write path)
  4. Worked examples
  5. Structure, updates and deletes
  6. Reading the graph: spreading activation
  7. Learning over time: feedback, decay, review
  8. Cost and complexity
  9. Isolation and privacy
  10. Configuration
  11. API on every surface
  12. Limits and tuning
  13. Research basis

docs.title: 1. Quick start
docs.text:
Linking is on whenever the knowledge graph or the intelligence is on, so kioko.intelligent() has it - and so do kioko serve --intelligence and kioko ui --intelligence for the REST/MCP service and the console. A plain MemoryLayer() or kioko serve without it stores memories without linking them; connect() (or kioko connect) links them later.

import kioko

memory = kioko.intelligent()                      # or MemoryLayer(auto_link=True)
U = "kumar"

memory.goals.add("Ship the Kioko memory layer by December 15", user_id=U)
memory.graph.add("Kioko", "uses", "pgvector", user_id=U)          # entity graph
memory.manage("We decided to use pgvector because we already run Postgres.", user_id=U)
# linked: decision "use pgvector because we already run Postgres" serves goal "Ship the Kioko memory layer..."

memory.add("Line 3 keeps faulting with error E-217.", user_id=U, memory_type="episodic", session_id="s1")
memory.add("Found it: the encoder cable on line 3 was loose.", user_id=U, memory_type="episodic", session_id="s1")
# linked: event "Found it: the encoder cable on line 3 was loose" resolves event "Line 3 keeps faulting..."

for link in memory.graph.links(goal_id):            # every link, with its evidence
    print(link.line(), "|", link.why, link.weight, link.by)

memory.graph.related(memory_id)                    # what is connected, best first, with the path
memory.graph.explain(a, b)                         # why two memories are (or are not) linked
ctx = memory.recall("line 3 is faulting with E-217 again", user_id=U)
print(ctx.text)                                    # ... and a "How these memories connect:" section

recall() follows the links: a question that retrieves one memory also brings the memories most strongly connected to it, and the memory block tells the agent how they connect:

Relevant memories:
- Line 3 keeps faulting with error E-217.
- Found it: the encoder cable on line 3 was loose.
- The line 3 conveyor jammed twice this morning.

Procedures that may apply:
- Clear a conveyor jam on line 3: 1) Press stop; 2) Open the guard; 3) Remove the jammed bottle; 4) Reset the drive

Lessons from earlier attempts:
- For clearing conveyor jams: reset the drive before reopening the guard (1/1 worked). Lesson: always check the photo-eye alignment after a jam

How these memories connect:
- lesson "For clearing conveyor jams: reset the drive before reopenin…" refines procedure "Clear a conveyor jam on line 3"
- event "Found it: the encoder cable on line 3 was loose" resolves event "Line 3 keeps faulting with error E-217"
- event "Found it: the encoder cable on line 3 was loose" resolves event "The line 3 conveyor jammed twice this morning"
- procedure "Clear a conveyor jam on line 3" applies to event "The line 3 conveyor jammed twice this morning"
- event "Line 3 keeps faulting with error E-217" follows event "The line 3 conveyor jammed twice this morning"

(The output above is real, from the memories tests/test_memory_graph.py seeds; the lesson was not retrieved by the question's words, it was brought in by its link to the procedure.)

Memories written before linking was on are linked with memory.graph.connect(user_id=...), kioko connect, or the console's Link unlinked memories button. The maintenance pass (memory.maintain()) does it as well.

docs.title: 2. What a link is
docs.text:
A link is a typed, weighted connection between two memories, read as a sentence: source <type> target.

MemoryLink(source="d1", target="g1", type="serves", weight=0.6, why="via Kioko uses pgvector", by="auto",
           source_label="use pgvector because we already run Postgres", source_type="decision",
           target_label="Ship the Kioko memory layer by December 15", target_type="goal")
# line(): decision "use pgvector because we already run Postgres" serves goal "Ship the Kioko memory layer by December 15"

docs.title: Link types
docs.text: Type Reads as Typical pair (source -> target) Made by serves serves decision / procedure / skill -> goal algorithm advances advances event with progress or a fix -> goal ("finished the analysis") algorithm concerns concerns other event -> goal (a fault on the line the goal is about) algorithm informs informs knowledge / fact / preference / insight / event -> decision, procedure, skill, lesson algorithm refines refines lesson -> procedure / skill / decision algorithm learned_from was learned from lesson -> event algorithm applies_to applies to procedure / skill -> event algorithm resolves resolves fix -> problem (event with a fix cue -> event with a problem cue; a procedure that worked -> the incident) algorithm, feedback follows follows later event -> earlier event of the same session algorithm part_of is part of sub-goal -> goal structure supersedes supersedes new decision -> the decision it replaced structure derived_from is derived from insight / episode summary -> its evidence structure related_to is related to anything else, or when only the entity graph connects them algorithm, manual

docs.title: Who made it
docs.text:
by Meaning Fades? Counts towards the degree cap? structure follows from the memory's own fields (a goal's parent, a decision's supersedes, an insight's evidence) no no manual memory.graph.link(), POST /v1/memories/{id}/links, kioko link, the console no no feedback a fix that worked (section 7) yes no llm confirmed or retyped by a model review yes yes auto the linking algorithm yes yes

Between two memories there is at most one link. A weaker author never replaces a stronger one's link (the order is the table's order); the same author's newer link replaces the older one. Asking for a link by hand where a stronger one exists (a sub-goal is already part_of its goal) raises LinkConflict (REST: 409) instead of pretending it was stored; asking again for a link that is already there just returns it.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Links live in each memory's metadata as an adjacency list, written on both memories:

"links": [
  {"id": "9f2c…", "type": "resolves", "dir": "out", "w": 0.677, "by": "auto",
   "why": "shared: line 3; similar meaning (0.30); a problem and its fix; same session, 0 min apart",
   "at": 1793135275.85, "seen": 1793135275.85}
],
"entities": ["line 3"],
"linked_at": 1793135275.85

dir is out on the source and in on the target. entities caches what the memory is about and linked_at marks that the linker has seen it. Because links are ordinary metadata, every store supports them (in-process, SQLite, pgvector, Qdrant, the REST service), they travel with exports and backups, and reading a memory's links costs no extra query. Entries that are not link dictionaries (say, your own "links": ["https://…"]) are left alone.

docs.title: 3. The linking algorithm (write path)
docs.text:
Every write that creates a memory (add, learn, manage, any kind's add/record/reflect) ends with linker.on_write(memory, "added"). A content change re-derives the memory's automatic links; a metadata-only change checks its structural links. Linking never breaks a write: an error is logged and the write stands.

              new memory m
                   |
   (1) ANCHOR      |  entities E(m), salient terms S(m), IDF weights
                   v
   (2) CANDIDATES  |  inverted index (rare shared terms, bridged entities) + nearest neighbours
                   |  + same session + structural targets          (<= ~50 memories)
                   v
   (3) EVIDENCE    |  share, sem, bridge, time, cue   for each candidate c
                   v
   (4) COMBINE     |  score = prior(kind m, kind c) * noisy-OR(evidence)
                   v
   (5) GATE+SELECT |  concrete evidence and score >= 0.35; best 5
                   v
   (6) TYPE        |  pair of kinds + cue words -> serves / resolves / refines / ...
                   v
   (7) STORE       |  both adjacency lists (one owner), degree cap 12, one transaction

docs.title: Step 0: which memories take part
docs.text: Linkable kinds: facts and preferences (not profile.* slots: they are in every context anyway), episodes, knowledge, goals, procedures, skills, lessons (strategies), decisions and summaries (insights and episode summaries; not a session's rolling summary). Instructions, working memory, graph triples, entities and the layer's bookkeeping are not linked.

docs.title: Step 1: anchor - what the memory is about
docs.text:
Entities E(m), each a lower-case key:

  • identifiers: tickets and work orders (INC-4521), error codes (E-217), part and model numbers (S7-1500), addresses (10.20.0.0/16);
  • assets with a number: line 3, press 12, cell 4B, server 2 ...;
  • names: sequences of capitalised words (Rockwell Automation, FactoryTalk Optix, OPC UA). The first word of a sentence counts only if it is distinctive (ALLCAPS, CamelCase, contains a digit); framing words (User, Decision, Goal, Lesson, month and day names ...) never count; after a framing prefix ("Goal: Ship ...") an action verb is dropped;
  • entities the user's entity graph already knows (graph.match_entities), so lower-case names like pgvector count once the graph has them.

Salient terms S(m): the entity keys (as e:<key>) plus the memory's content words, stemmed, without stop words, digits, the framing vocabulary of stored memories ("decided", "lesson", "prefers" ...) and light verbs ("keeps", "came", "went", "got" ...) (t:<stem>). "The fault came back" and "the theme came up" share nothing.

IDF weights. The linker keeps, per (user, agent) scope, the number of linkable memories n and each term's document frequency df(t), incrementally:

idf(t) = ln(1 + (n + 20 - df(t) + 0.5) / (df(t) + 0.5))     (BM25's IDF, smoothed with 20 virtual memories)
idf(t) = 0      if n >= 20 and df(t) / n > 0.5               (a term in most memories connects nothing)
w(t)   = idf(t) * 1.5 if t is an entity, else idf(t)

The 20 virtual memories (that contain none of the terms) keep a young store from treating every shared word as common: with two memories, plain IDF would give a shared word almost no weight; smoothed, the words weigh almost evenly until real statistics take over.

The same structure is an inverted index: postings(t) = the memories that contain t. It is built once per scope from the store (cached for 10 minutes, updated on every write) and is what makes candidate search cheap.

docs.title: Step 2: candidates - who could be linked
docs.text:
1. Inverted index. The 12 terms of S(m) with the highest IDF, plus the entities the graph relates to E(m) (step 3, bridge), vote for the memories in their postings, each vote weighted by w(t). A term with more than max(50, 0.2 n) postings nominates nothing. The 24 memories with the most votes become candidates; the shared knowledge base (@shared) adds up to 12.
  2. Meaning. A vector database (pgvector, Qdrant) adds its 24 nearest neighbours. On a store without vector search, a semantic embedder adds the hybrid search's top 24 (a full scan); the offline embedder is lexical, so the inverted index has already found what it would.
  3. Same session. Up to 30 memories written in the same session.
  4. Structure. The memories the new memory's fields name (step 5).

Candidates of another user, of another agent of this user, or chunks of the same ingested document are discarded here.

docs.title: Step 3: evidence - for each candidate c
docs.text:
Signal Definition Range share weighted overlap of salient terms: W(S(m) ∩ S(c)) / min(W(S(m)), W(S(c))), W(X) = Σ w(t); halved (once) when every shared term is a hub (df >= max(4, 0.15 n)) or only names a place or machine ("line 3", "station 12") and its words: where something happened is weak common ground - two faults on line 3 may be unrelated - while what it is about ("Nike Pegasus", "E-217") is strong 0..1 sem meaning, calibrated to the embedder: clamp((cos - h/2) / (h/2), 0, 1), h = the ranker's min_vector_only (0.3 by default; tune it for your embedder) 0..1 bridge the entity graph relates an entity of one memory to an entity of the other that the first does not mention (Kioko -uses-> pgvector): 1.0, or 0.4 when either entity is a hub (df >= max(4, 0.15 n)); 0 when they already share the entity 0, 0.4, 1 time same session, written within 2 hours: 1.0; same session: 0.5; else 0 0..1 cue a problem and its fix: the type rule says resolves (step 6), same session within 2 hours, and at least one shared term 0, 1

The weighted overlap coefficient (rather than Jaccard) lets a short memory match a long one ("User likes green tea" vs a paragraph about tea), and IDF makes rare terms - an error code, a product name - count far more than common ones.

docs.title: Step 4: combine
docs.text:
Each signal is independent evidence that the two memories belong together; they are combined with a noisy-OR and scaled by a prior for the pair of kinds:

raw   = 1 - (1 - 0.8·share) · (1 - ω·sem) · (1 - 0.6·bridge) · (1 - 0.35·time) · (1 - 0.5·cue)
score = prior(kind(m), kind(c)) · raw                 ω = 0.5, or 0.25 with a lexical embedder

With the offline embedder, similarity is itself computed from words, so it repeats share and counts half.

Priors (symmetric; the kinds are the nouns used in link lines):

Pair Prior Pair Prior decision - goal 1.00 event - event 0.85 lesson - procedure 1.00 event - decision 0.85 lesson - skill 0.90 knowledge - procedure 0.85 lesson - event 0.90 knowledge - decision 0.85 event - procedure 0.90 procedure - skill 0.85 event - insight 0.90 lesson - decision 0.85 procedure - goal 0.85 goal - goal 0.80 event - goal 0.85 decision - decision, decision - procedure 0.80 skill - goal, fact - goal, lesson - goal, insight - goal 0.70 facts, knowledge and the rest 0.60 - 0.75 anything with a preference 0.50 not listed 0.60

docs.title: Step 5: gate and select
docs.text:
A candidate is linked only with concrete evidence and a high enough score:

evidence = share >= 0.30
        or cos >= h + (1 - h)/2                          (very similar meaning: 0.65 at h = 0.3)
        or bridge = 1 and the pair is means -> end      (decision/procedure/skill/event -> goal)
        or cue = 1
        or share >= 0.15 and (sem >= 0.5 or time = 1 or bridge > 0)
linked   = evidence and score >= threshold               (threshold = 0.35)

Similarity alone never links two memories (unless very high): with the offline embedder, "ops prefers one database" and "User prefers Python" score 0.25 cosine on the word prefers alone. A graph bridge alone links only a means to its end; elsewhere it supports other evidence. The best max_new = 5 candidates by score are linked, plus every structural target.

docs.title: Step 6: type
docs.text:
The pair of kinds decides the type; cue words refine it:

Pair Type (direction) decision - goal decision serves goal procedure / skill - goal procedure serves goal event - goal event advances goal if it reports progress or a fix (finished, shipped, passed, 60 %, fixed ...) and no problem; otherwise concerns knowledge / fact / preference / insight / lesson - goal informs goal lesson - procedure / skill / decision lesson refines it lesson - event lesson learned_from event procedure / skill - event procedure applies_to event event - decision event informs decision event - event resolves when one has a fix cue (fixed, found it, root cause, was loose, replaced ...), the other a problem cue (fault, error, failed, jammed, keeps …ing ...) and the fix was recorded after the problem (a fault that comes back after a fix is not resolved by it); else follows (later -> earlier) within a session; else related_to knowledge / fact / preference / insight - decision / procedure / skill / lesson informs anything else (including insight - event / fact) related_to

derived_from is never guessed from content: it is claimed only where the provenance is recorded (an insight's evidence list, a summary's episodes), as a structural link.

When only the entity graph connects two memories (little shared text, no session), the link is typed related_to - except a means serving its end, which keeps serves / advances / concerns. The type says no more than the evidence supports.

docs.title: Step 7: store
docs.text: The link is added to both memories' adjacency lists in one transaction (update_many on SQLite), with its evidence in why and the score as weight. A memory keeps at most max_degree = 12 automatic links (auto, llm): when a new link would exceed that, the weakest (faded weight, section 7) gives way on both sides. One event, memory.linked, reports the new links (the console's Activity and Playground show it; a ManageReport lists it as linked: ...).

docs.title: 4. Worked examples
docs.text:
All numbers below are what the algorithm computes for the memories of section 1 (9 linkable memories, offline embedder, h = 0.3). memory.graph.explain(a, b) prints the same.

A fix and its problem. "Found it: the encoder cable on line 3 was loose." vs "Line 3 keeps faulting with error E-217." (same session):

salient weights  fix:   e:line 3 2.85, found 3.0, encoder 3.0, cable 3.0, line 1.9, loose 3.0       W = 16.75
                 fault: e:e-217 4.49, e:line 3 2.85, line 1.9, fault 3.0, error 3.0                W = 15.24
share = (2.85 + 1.9) / min(16.75, 15.24) = 0.312, halved: line 3 is in 4 of the 9 memories (a hub) -> 0.156
sem   = clamp((0.301 - 0.15) / 0.15) = 1.0       time = 1 (same session, 0 min apart)     cue = 1
raw   = 1 - (1 - 0.8·0.156)(1 - 0.25·1)(1 - 0)(1 - 0.35·1)(1 - 0.5·1) = 0.787
score = prior(event, event) 0.85 · 0.787 = 0.669  -> linked: event "Found it …" resolves event "Line 3 keeps …"
why   = "shared: line 3; similar meaning (0.30); a problem and its fix; same session, 0 min apart"

The shared words alone would not have been enough (share 0.156 < 0.3); a problem and its fix in the same session, the fix recorded after the problem, are.

A means and its end, through the entity graph. "Decision: Vector database - chose pgvector because we already run Postgres." vs "Goal: Ship the Kioko memory layer by December 15.": no shared word (cosine 0.04), but the decision mentions pgvector, the goal mentions Kioko, and the entity graph holds Kioko -uses-> pgvector:

bridge = 1.0 (neither entity is a hub)    raw = 1 - (1 - 0.6) = 0.6    score = prior(decision, goal) 1.0 · 0.6 = 0.60
-> linked: decision "use pgvector …" serves goal "Ship the Kioko memory layer …"     why = "via Kioko uses pgvector"

A lesson and a procedure. share 0.487 (drive, clearing, reset), cosine 0.47: raw = 1 - (1 - 0.39)(1 - 0.25) = 0.542, prior 1.0 -> 0.542: lesson refines procedure.

Not linked. "User likes green tea." vs "The plant's PLC network uses the 10.20.0.0/16 subnet.": nothing shared, cosine 0.03 -> raw 0, no link.

A hub does not bridge everything. With Line 3 -has-> conveyor in the entity graph and "line 3" mentioned by many memories, a telemetry note about line 3 and a lesson about conveyor jams are not linked: the bridge through the hub counts 0.4, and a bridge alone links only a means to its end.

On a mixed set of 35 memories (a work project, plant operations, running, tea), the algorithm made 19 links, all of which a reader would accept (the weakest: "User drinks coffee before long runs" informs the decision about running shoes, 0.39). Before the hub, lexical-embedder and type rules above were added, the same set produced 38 links, about a third of them spurious.

docs.title: 5. Structure, updates and deletes
docs.text:
Structural links follow from a memory's own fields and never fade:

  • a goal with parent -> part_of the parent goal;
  • a decision with supersedes -> supersedes the old decision. The new decision answers the same question, so it takes over the old decision's other links (the goal it served, the benchmark that informed it), at 90 % of their weight and with why = "taken over from the decision it replaced (...)". Links the algorithm made move: the old decision keeps only its supersedes link to its replacement (plus any link a person or feedback made, which the new decision also gets), so a goal's neighbourhood holds the current decision, not two competing ones - also when the new decision had already found the goal by itself (then the old link just goes). A taken-over link is marked with from = the replaced decision. From then on the replaced decision is history: it is never a candidate for another memory's automatic links, and whatever the algorithm finds for it later (a connect() backfill of memories written before linking was on, a rebuild) is linked to the decision that replaced it - the newest one in the chain - marked from, never to the replaced one; The old decision is history one hop further away - trace and the console still reach it - and recall leaves superseded decisions out;
  • an insight with evidence (reflection) or an episode summary with episodes (consolidation) -> derived_from each of them.

Updates. New content (update(content=...), a same-key update, a contradiction that supersedes a fact) drops the memory's automatic links and derives them again from the new text: its mentions are extracted again and its entries in the term statistics are replaced (a memory that no longer mentions DB-17 is no longer found through it). Links a decision took over from the decision it replaced are kept: they cannot be derived again, so neither an edit nor connect(rebuild=True) removes them (only deleting a memory does). A metadata-only change checks the structural links; the takeover happens once per replacement, so a link someone removed stays removed.

Deletes. The deleted memory's neighbours forget their links to it. Links that point at memories removed behind the layer's back (another process, a raw store call) are skipped when read and removed by prune().

Merges. When consolidation merges a near-duplicate into an older memory, the duplicate's links move to the survivor before it is deleted.

docs.title: 6. Reading the graph: spreading activation
docs.text:
recall() retrieves memories as usual (hybrid dense + BM25 + entity graph + recency, fused with RRF, planned by intent). Then it spreads activation from what it retrieved to the memories linked to it - a personalized PageRank over the linked neighbourhood:

seeds       s(v) ∝ retrieval score of each retrieved memory (and of each open goal the question is about)
neighbourhood: breadth first from the seeds, 2 hops, the 8 strongest links per memory, at most 40 memories,
               links whose faded weight is below 0.1 are not followed; superseded decisions pass on 30 %
edge weight  a(u, v) = faded weight of the link (section 7), symmetric
transition   P(u -> v) = a(u, v) / Σ_x a(u, x)
iterate      p ← α · s + (1 - α) · Pᵀ p          α = 0.5 (restart), 20 iterations
             a memory without links sends its mass back to the seeds
select       the non-seed memories with the most activation that the context may show
             (same filters as retrieval: not superseded, not consolidated into the model, in scope -
             the user's own memories, and shared knowledge only when include_shared is on)

The best links of them (default 3, or the plan's number) join the section of their kind (procedures, decisions, ...) with signals["linked"] = activation relative to the strongest seed. They count as shown, not used: their access count does not grow, so association never heats a memory up on its own (the same rule as for pinned memories).

Open goals are always in the context. They seed the expansion when the question names them (shares a word) or is about goals ("how are my goals going?"), so a goal's decisions and procedures come along.

The links section. Whatever links is, the context's links section lists the links among the memories it contains that touch a memory the question retrieved or the links brought in - first the links that brought a memory in, then relations before provenance (derived_from says where a summary came from, not why a memory matters), then structural, feedback and manual links, then by weight; at most 6 lines, and no memory takes more than two of them while other links are waiting. Links among memories that are always there (open goals, profile, pins) are left out unless the question is about them: for "why does line 3 keep faulting?" a goal and its sub-goal explain nothing, for "how are my goals going?" they do. Under a token budget the section is filled after decisions; a line whose memories were left out is dropped.

How many linked memories a question gets is part of the recall plan:

Intent links Intent links relational ("who is Krutika?") 6 temporal 2 decision ("why did we pick X?") 4 knowledge 2 goals 4 skills 2 how-to 3 personal 1 strategy 3 small talk, feedback 0 (no expansion, no links section) general (no intent) 3

Other reads: related(memory_id, depth=2) runs the same activation from one memory and returns each related memory with the chain of links that reaches it; trace(a, b) is the shortest chain between two memories (breadth first); explain(a, b) scores a pair from scratch.

docs.title: 7. Learning over time: feedback, decay, review
docs.text:
Feedback makes the strongest links. With an intelligence, when the user says a suggestion worked ("that worked, thanks"), the procedure, skill or lesson that was credited is linked to the problems of the session it solved: episodes and facts of the same session from the last 6 hours with a problem cue, plus problem episodes the agent was shown. The link is fix resolves problem, weight 0.8, by = feedback. Next time the problem comes up, recall brings the fix and says why.

Hebbian reinforcement. On the same success, the links among the memories the agent was given are strengthened - "memories that are used together, link together":

w ← w + 0.2 · (1 - w),   seen = now

Decay. Automatic, model-reviewed and feedback links fade unless they are used:

faded weight = w · 0.5 ^ (days since seen / 180)          (structure and manual links do not fade)

prune() removes links whose faded weight is below 0.1 and links to memories that no longer exist. The degree cap always lets the weakest automatic link go first.

Model review (optional). With Intelligence(llm=...), the maintenance task shows the model the 12 most recent automatic links in one call:

p1: A = [decision] 'Decision: Vector database - chose pgvector because we already run Postgres.'
    B = [goal] 'Goal: Ship the Kioko memory layer by December 15.'
    proposed: A serves B (via Kioko uses pgvector)
...
Answer with JSON only: {"links": [{"pair": "p1", "keep": true, "type": "serves", "source": "A", "why": "..."}]}

It keeps, retypes or drops each link; kept links become by = llm with weight at least 0.7. Invalid pairs, types and malformed answers are ignored, and a failing model never breaks maintenance. One call reviews up to 12 links, so the cost stays small; links are made by the algorithm at write time either way.

When maintenance runs. Every link_every turns (25 by default) the scheduler links memories that were never linked (up to 200 per run), prunes, and - with a model - reviews. memory.maintain(tasks=["link"]), kioko maintain --tasks link and POST /v1/maintain {"tasks": ["link"]} run it now.

docs.title: 8. Cost and complexity
docs.text:
Per write, with T salient terms (typically 5-15) and at most C ≈ 50 candidates:

Step Cost anchor O(text) + graph entity matching candidates O(12 · postings) votes, ≤ 36 store reads; a vector database adds one k-NN query evidence O(C · T) plus C cosines store 1 + (links made) records written in one transaction

Per recall with links > 0: at most 40 memory reads around the seeds and 20 PageRank iterations over at most 40 nodes; nothing at all when the retrieved memories have no links.

Measured with python examples/benchmarks/memory_graph_bench.py (SQLite, offline embedder, synthetic notes on 20 topics, so most notes have related notes - the dense, expensive case; median of 40 writes and 30 recalls):

memories write, linking off write, linking on recall, links=0 recall, links=3 connect() links per memory (mean / max) 500 5 ms 21 ms 183 ms 181 ms 2479 links in 11 s (22 ms each) 6.4 / 12 2000 6 ms 20 ms 710 ms 707 ms 10000 links in 66 s (33 ms each) 6.5 / 12

The write cost does not grow with the store: candidates come from the inverted index, not from a scan. About half of it is SQLite committing (your disk's fsync speed matters). Following links added no measurable time to a recall in these runs (the difference is within run-to-run noise): the expansion reads at most 40 memories. Recall itself grows with the store on SQLite because it scores every memory in scope; on pgvector or Qdrant the database does the nearest-neighbour search, so recall and linking should stay bounded there (not measured: these numbers are from SQLite only).

docs.title: 9. Isolation and privacy
docs.text:
• A link only ever connects memories of one user; for an agent-scoped memory, of the same agent.
  • Links to the shared knowledge base (@shared) are stored only on the user's memory: nothing about a user is written into shared data, and another user's recall can never follow such a link back.
  • Profile slots are not linked; secrets never become memories in the first place (DropSecrets).
  • Deleting a memory removes it from its neighbours' lists; forget requests delete memories the same way.

docs.title: 10. Configuration
docs.text:
MemoryLayer(auto_link=True,                      # default: on with auto_graph or an intelligence
            linker={"threshold": 0.35, "max_new": 5, "max_degree": 12})

MemoryLinker(memory, threshold=0.35,   # minimum score for an automatic link
             max_new=5,                # links per new memory
             max_degree=12,            # automatic links per memory
             candidates=24,            # candidates from the inverted index / vector search
             half_life_days=180,       # fading of automatic and feedback links
             min_weight=0.1,           # below this a link is pruned and not followed
             restart=0.5, iterations=20, fanout=8, max_nodes=40)   # spreading activation

Intelligence(link_every=25,            # maintenance: link, prune, review
             link_review=12,           # links the model reviews per run (with llm=)
             ...)

memory.recall(q, links=0)              # no expansion for one call; the plan decides otherwise
memory.context(q, links=3)             # context() expands only when asked (default 0)

kioko.intelligence.planner.LINKS_PER_INTENT holds the per-intent numbers of section 6. HybridRanker( min_vector_only=...) sets h, the similarity scale of step 3: with OpenAI or Azure OpenAI embeddings, a value around 0.45 matches their cosine range better than the default 0.3.

docs.title: 11. API on every surface
docs.text:
Python (memory.graph, also on memory.scoped(...) and RemoteMemory):

Call Returns link(a, b, type="related_to", weight=1.0, why="") MemoryLink (manual, never fades) unlink(a, b) True if they were linked links(memory_id) [MemoryLink], strongest first related(memory_id, depth=2, limit=10) [RelatedMemory(record, score, path)] trace(a, b, max_depth=4) [MemoryLink] from a to b explain(a, b) LinkScore(score, linked, type, why, signals) connect(user_id=..., rebuild=False, limit=None) {"memories", "links", "dropped", "duration_ms"} memories(user_id=..., center=None, depth=2, limit=120) {"nodes", "edges", "stats"} for drawing

REST (/v1, documented in /v1/openapi.json under the graph tag):

GET    /v1/memories/{id}/links                       the links of a memory
POST   /v1/memories/{id}/links    {"target", "type", "why", "weight"}      link by hand (409: a stronger link exists)
DELETE /v1/memories/{id}/links/{target}              unlink
GET    /v1/memories/{id}/links/{target}/explain      the evidence between two memories
GET    /v1/memories/{id}/related?depth=2&limit=10    spreading activation from one memory
GET    /v1/graph/memories?user_id=&center=&depth=    nodes and edges
POST   /v1/graph/connect          {"user_id", "rebuild", "limit"}           link what was never linked
POST   /v1/recall                 {"query", "user_id", "links": 3}          (the plan sets links when omitted)

CLI

kioko related <memory-id> [--depth 2] [--json]      # links and what is connected, with the path
kioko link <a> <b> --type resolves --why "..."      # by hand; --remove to unlink
kioko connect --user kumar [--rebuild]              # link memories written before linking was on
kioko maintain --tasks link                         # link, prune and (with a model) review

MCP: the explore_memories tool finds the memory that best matches a query and lists what is linked to it, with the evidence; get_memory_context already includes linked memories and the links section.

Console: the Graph tab's Memory graph view draws memories as nodes (coloured by kind) and links as edges (dashed: structure; green: a fix that worked). Click a memory to see each link with its evidence, weight and author, what lies further away (with the chain of links), and to centre on it or unlink. Link unlinked memories runs connect(). The Playground shows the links each turn made, and the Recall tab shows the links section and the linked signal.

docs.title: 12. Limits and tuning
docs.text:
• Cue words are English. Problem / fix / progress cues and the type rules are English; in other languages links are still made (shared terms, entities, meaning, sessions) but typed related_to more often. A model review retypes them.
  • The offline embedder is lexical. "car" and "automobile" share nothing; with a semantic embedder, set h (the ranker's min_vector_only) to your embedder's cosine range and paraphrases link too.
  • Tune the threshold, not the weights. Raise threshold (0.45) for a sparser, more certain graph; lower it (0.3) for more associations. max_new and max_degree bound the cost either way.
  • Bulk imports. Linking adds a few milliseconds per memory on a vector database and tens of milliseconds on SQLite (section 8). For a large import, write with auto_link=False and run connect() afterwards - same result, with progress you can report.
  • Concurrent writers. Adjacency lists are updated under the layer's write lock. Several processes writing the same memories can, rarely, lose a link update (last writer wins); connect(rebuild=True) re-derives everything.

docs.title: 13. Research basis
docs.text:
The design combines well-studied ideas; Kioko's contribution is making them work offline, cheaply, and on any store.

  • A-MEM (Xu et al., 2025; NeurIPS 2025, arXiv:2502.12110). Zettelkasten-style agent memory: when a note is added, the most similar existing notes are retrieved (embedding similarity, top-k) and an LLM decides which links to create; "memory evolution" can then update the context, keywords and tags of the retrieved neighbours. Kioko's write-time linking follows this shape, with an algorithmic judge (steps 3-6) by default and the model as an optional reviewer (section 7).
  • HippoRAG (Gutiérrez et al., 2024; NeurIPS 2024, arXiv:2405.14831) builds a knowledge graph from passages and, at query time, runs Personalized PageRank seeded on the query's nodes (damping / restart 0.5) to find passages in one multi-hop step. HippoRAG 2 (arXiv:2502.14802, ICML 2025) adds passage nodes to the graph next to phrase nodes. Kioko's recall expansion is PPR over memory nodes, seeded with the retrieved memories, with the same restart probability.
  • Zep / Graphiti (Rasmussen et al., 2025, arXiv:2501.13956): a temporal knowledge graph for agent memory with episode, semantic-entity and community subgraphs and bi-temporal edges that are invalidated, not deleted, when contradicted. Kioko's entity graph keeps the history of single-valued relations the same way, and superseded decisions stay in the memory graph as history, one supersedes link behind the decision that replaced them.
  • Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025; ECAI 2025, arXiv:2504.19413). Its graph variant, Mem0^g, stores memories as a directed labelled graph of entities and relationships, with a conflict detector and an LLM update resolver that mark obsolete relationships invalid.
  • GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024, arXiv:2404.16130): an LLM-built entity graph, hierarchical Leiden communities and pre-generated community summaries for global questions. Kioko's console groups memories by connected cluster; community summaries are not part of Kioko.
  • Generative Agents (Park et al., 2023; UIST '23, arXiv:2304.03442): reflections cite the memories they are based on ("insight (because of 1, 5, 3)") - Kioko's derived_from links; retrieval scores recency (from last access), importance and relevance.
  • Spreading activation (Collins & Loftus, 1975, Psychological Review 82(6), 407-428, doi:10.1037/0033-295X.82.6.407): activation spreads from a concept to related concepts along weighted links and fades with distance.
  • Personalized PageRank: suggested by Page, Brin, Motwani & Winograd (Stanford TR 1999-66) and first worked out by Haveliwala, "Topic-sensitive PageRank" (WWW 2002, doi:10.1145/511446.511513) and Jeh & Widom, "Scaling personalized web search" (WWW 2003, doi:10.1145/775152.775191).
  • Hebbian learning (D. O. Hebb, The Organization of Behavior, Wiley, 1949); the phrase "cells that fire together wire together" was popularised by Shatz (Scientific American, 1992; see also Löwel & Singer, Science, 1992). Kioko strengthens links among memories that were used together successfully.
  • BM25's IDF (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009) weights the salient terms, and Reciprocal Rank Fusion (Cormack, Clarke & Büttcher, SIGIR 2009, doi:10.1145/1571941.1572114, k = 60) fuses Kioko's retrievers before the expansion.
  • MemoryOS ("Memory OS of AI Agent", Kang et al.; EMNLP 2025, arXiv:2506.06326) promotes segments by heat (retrievals + page count + recency); Kioko's pinning uses the same idea, and linked memories are deliberately excluded from it (section 6).
  • Related agent-memory graphs: AriGraph (Anokhin et al., IJCAI 2025, arXiv:2407.04363) combines semantic and episodic memories in one graph built while the agent explores; SynapticRAG (Hou et al., Findings of ACL 2025, arXiv:2410.13553) retrieves dialogue memories by propagating activation between them.

docs.title: Kioko guide: add memory to your agent
docs.text:
This guide takes a new user from installation to a production setup. It follows one realistic project throughout: a plant support assistant for controls engineers that remembers who each engineer is, what they are working towards, which procedures fix which faults, what the team decided, and what worked.

  1. Install
  2. Your first memory
  3. The agent loop
  4. Attach to a framework
  5. Persist it
  6. Tell it things directly
  7. Let a model manage memory
  8. Run it as a service
  9. MCP hosts
  10. Look inside: the console
  11. Keep it healthy
  12. Production checklist
  13. Configuration reference
  14. Troubleshooting

The other documents go deeper: memory types covers each of the 15 kinds, intelligence the self-managing mode, stores SQLite, pgvector and Qdrant, console the web UI, and the cookbook has runnable recipes with their output.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
Kioko needs Python 3.14 or newer. The core has no dependencies: storage, the offline embedder, the extraction rules, the intelligence, the REST and MCP server and the web console all use the standard library.

pip install kioko                 # the core
pip install "kioko[pgvector]"     # + Postgres / pgvector (psycopg)
pip install "kioko[agno]"         # + the Agno adapter
pip install .                     # or from the source folder

On Windows, use the launcher: py -3.14 -m pip install .... To check the installation, run kioko demo. It runs a scripted conversation with the offline demo agent.

docs.title: 2. Your first memory (five lines)
docs.text:
import kioko

memory = kioko.intelligent("sqlite:///plant-memory.db")      # a file next to your code; nothing else to set up

# After each exchange, hand the turn to Kioko. It decides what is worth keeping, and where.
memory.record_turn("Hi, I'm Asha, a controls engineer at the Pune plant. I prefer short answers.",
                   "Nice to meet you, Asha!", user_id="asha", session_id="mon-shift")
memory.record_turn("My goal is to get line 3 OEE above 85% by December 31.",
                   "Noted - let's track it.", user_id="asha", session_id="mon-shift")
memory.record_turn("To reset the safety relay, switch off the main breaker, then press reset for 5 seconds, "
                   "then switch the breaker back on.", "Thanks, saved.", user_id="asha", session_id="mon-shift")

# Before each answer, ask Kioko what the agent should know.
ctx = memory.recall("The safety relay tripped again - what do I do?", user_id="asha", session_id="tue-shift")
print(ctx.text)

Output:

<memory>
Long-term memory about the user. Use it to personalise your answer. If it conflicts with the user's latest message, trust the latest message. Do not mention this block unless asked.

Instructions from the user:
- User prefers short answers.

About the user:
- User is a controls engineer.
- User works at the Pune plant.
- User's name is Asha.

The user's open goals:
- Get line 3 OEE above 85% by December 31 (medium, 0%, due 2026-12-31)

Procedures that may apply:
- reset the safety relay: 1) Switch off the main breaker; 2) Press reset for 5 seconds; 3) Switch the breaker back on
</memory>

Each part of the conversation went to the kind of memory where it belongs:

  • name, role and employer became profile slots;
  • "I prefer short answers" is about how to answer, so it became a standing instruction;
  • the goal became a goal with a due date;
  • the how-to became a procedure with ordered steps.

The question the next day was recognised as a how-to, so the procedure was retrieved first. Nothing was configured, and no model was called. That is kioko.intelligent(): see intelligence.

Prefer full control? kioko.MemoryLayer.sqlite("plant-memory.db") gives you the same memory without the self-management. learn() then extracts with rules, and recall() retrieves every kind with fixed caps. You can switch at any time with MemoryLayer(..., intelligence=True).

docs.title: 3. The agent loop
docs.text:
Whatever your agent looks like, memory takes three lines per turn: recall → answer → record.

import kioko

memory = kioko.intelligent("sqlite:///plant-memory.db")
user, session = "asha", "tue-shift"


def call_llm(system: str, user_message: str) -> str:
    """Stand-in for your model call (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, a local model ...)."""
    return f"[model answer, using {system.count(chr(10) + '- ')} memory lines]"


def answer(message: str) -> str:
    ctx = memory.recall(message, user_id=user, session_id=session)                       # 1. remember
    reply = call_llm("You are a plant support assistant.\n\n" + ctx.text, message)       # 2. answer
    memory.record_turn(message, reply, user_id=user, session_id=session)                 # 3. learn
    return reply


for message in ["The safety relay on line 3 tripped again, ticket INC-7731.",
                "That worked, thanks!",
                "We switched the line 3 HMI from PanelView to FactoryTalk Optix because of remote access.",
                "I'm about 40% of the way to the OEE target."]:
    print(f"asha  > {message}\nagent > {answer(message)}")

print("\nworking memory:", memory.working(session, user_id=user).snapshot())
print("goal:", memory.goals.active(user_id=user)[0].line())
print("procedure track record:", memory.procedures.list(user_id=user)[0].successes, "success")
print("decisions:", [d.line() for d in memory.decisions.log(user_id=user)])

Output (after the five-line example above):

asha  > The safety relay on line 3 tripped again, ticket INC-7731.
agent > [model answer, using 6 memory lines]
asha  > That worked, thanks!
agent > [model answer, using 6 memory lines]
asha  > We switched the line 3 HMI from PanelView to FactoryTalk Optix because of remote access.
agent > [model answer, using 8 memory lines]
asha  > I'm about 40% of the way to the OEE target.
agent > [model answer, using 6 memory lines]

working memory: {'ticket': 'INC-7731'}
goal: Get line 3 OEE above 85% by December 31 (medium, 40%, due 2026-12-31)
procedure track record: 1 success
decisions: ['line 3 HMI: chose FactoryTalk Optix because of remote access (accepted 2026-10-27)']

Without being asked, Kioko:

  • kept the ticket number in the session's working memory;
  • credited "that worked" to the procedure the agent had just used;
  • logged the HMI decision with its reason;
  • moved the OEE goal to 40%.

With a real model, call_llm is a few lines. For example, with Azure OpenAI:

import os
from openai import AzureOpenAI

client = AzureOpenAI(azure_endpoint=os.environ["AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT"], api_version="2024-10-21")
# key: AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY, or azure_ad_token_provider=... for Entra ID

def call_llm(system: str, user_message: str) -> str:
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(model=os.environ["AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT"],
                                           messages=[{"role": "system", "content": system},
                                                     {"role": "user", "content": user_message}])
    return reply.choices[0].message.content

To get the most from provider prompt caching, use memory.kv.openai_messages(...) or memory.kv.anthropic_system(...). They put the stable part of the memory first, byte-identical from turn to turn (see KV-cache memory).

docs.title: 4. Attach to a framework instead
docs.text:
If your agent is built with a framework, attach() adds the same loop in one line. It recalls before each run and records after it:

from kioko import attach

agent = attach(agent, memory)                         # Agno agent: hooks + memory tools
graph = attach(graph, memory)                         # LangChain runnable / LangGraph graph (user and thread from config)
crew = attach(crew, memory, input_key="topic")        # CrewAI crew: which input holds the user's text
answer = attach(my_function, memory)                  # any function: answer(message, user_id=..., session_id=...)

It works with Agno, LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI, the OpenAI Agents SDK, AutoGen, smolagents, Semantic Kernel, your own classes and plain functions. For more control there are building blocks:

  • the @with_memory decorator;
  • MemoryMiddleware(memory).before(...) / .after(...);
  • memory.inject(messages, user_id=...) for OpenAI-style message lists;
  • memory.tools(user_id=...): save / search / update / delete tools your agent can call itself.

Attach to any agent has framework-specific notes, and examples/ has runnable examples (02_agno_agent.py, 03_any_agent.py, 05_frameworks_attach.py).

docs.title: 5. Persist it
docs.text:
The memory lives wherever the URL says. Change one string and the code stays the same:

memory = kioko.intelligent("sqlite:///plant-memory.db")                         # one file
memory = kioko.intelligent("postgresql://kioko:<password>@db:5432/kioko")      # Postgres + pgvector
memory = kioko.intelligent("qdrant://qdrant:6333/plant_memories")              # Qdrant
memory = kioko.connect("http://memory-service:8765")                           # a shared Kioko service

docker compose -f docker-compose.stores.yml up -d starts Postgres with pgvector, Qdrant and a Kioko service locally. Stores covers set-up, indexes, switching embedders (memory.reembed()) and writing your own store.

Use a semantic embedder in production. The default one is offline and lexical: it matches words, not meaning.

from kioko import AzureOpenAIEmbedder, OpenAIEmbedder

memory = kioko.intelligent("postgresql://...", embedder=AzureOpenAIEmbedder(deployment="text-embedding-3-small"))
memory = kioko.intelligent("postgresql://...", embedder=OpenAIEmbedder(model="text-embedding-3-small"))
memory = kioko.intelligent("postgresql://...", embedder=lambda texts: my_model.encode(texts).tolist())

docs.title: 6. Tell it things directly
docs.text:
Conversation fills memory by itself. When your code knows something, write it to the right kind directly. For example, to load the plant's runbooks into shared knowledge, or to record a decision from a change ticket:

memory.semantic.ingest(open("runbooks/line3.md").read(), source="line3-runbook", topic="operations")  # shared
memory.procedures.add("Recalibrate the line 3 encoder", user_id="asha",
                      steps=["Stop the line", "Run the calibration wizard", "Verify 10 cycles"])
memory.decisions.record("Historian", chosen="InfluxDB", rationale="retention policies", user_id="asha")
memory.goals.add("Cut changeover time to 15 minutes", user_id="asha", priority="high", due="2027-03-31")
memory.graph.add("Asha", "reports_to", "Ravi", user_id="asha")
memory.procedures.add_rule("Always cite the ticket number", user_id="asha")       # a standing instruction

Memory types describes all fifteen kinds and their APIs. Each kind has a runnable recipe in the cookbook.

docs.title: 7. Let a model manage memory
docs.text:
The offline intelligence covers common phrasings in English. For open-ended conversations, other languages, or subtler updates, give it a model. One call per turn decides every memory operation. Kioko still skips trivial turns without a call, validates what the model proposes, drops secrets, and falls back to the offline rules if the model fails.

def ask(prompt: str) -> str:                                   # any prompt -> text function
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(model=os.environ["AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT"], temperature=0,
                                           response_format={"type": "json_object"},
                                           messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return reply.choices[0].message.content

memory = kioko.intelligent("postgresql://...", llm=ask)        # routing, reflection and summaries use the model

Before you rely on it, preview what it decides:

report = memory.manage("Downtime is already down 12%.", user_id="asha", dry_run=True)
print(report.summary())       # goal.progress "Cut unplanned downtime on line 3 by 20%" -> 60%

Intelligence covers how both modes decide, the operations, the retrieval plans, maintenance, measured savings and the research behind it.

docs.title: How memories connect
docs.text:
With an intelligence (or auto_link=True), every memory is linked to related memories as it is written, and recall() follows the links. You don't have to do anything; it helps to know how to look:

for link in memory.graph.links(memory_id):
    print(link.line(), "-", link.why)
# decision "use pgvector because we already run Postgres" serves goal "Ship the Kioko memory layer ..." - via Kioko uses pgvector

memory.graph.related(memory_id)          # what is connected, best first, with the chain of links
memory.graph.connect(user_id="asha")     # link memories written before linking was on (once, after an import)

When a user tells the agent a fix worked, the fix is linked to the problem it solved; the next time the problem comes up, recall brings the fix along. The Graph tab of the console draws it all. Graph memory describes the algorithm.

docs.title: 8. Run it as a service (for any language)
docs.text:
When agents in several processes, containers or languages should share one memory, run it as a service. --intelligence makes the service manage memory by itself:

export KIOKO_API_KEY="$(python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))')"
kioko serve --store postgresql://kioko:<password>@db:5432/kioko --intelligence --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8765

REST API   http://localhost:8765/v1        (OpenAPI document: /v1/openapi.json)
MCP        http://localhost:8765/mcp

The agent loop is the same in every language: POST /v1/recall before the model call, POST /v1/turns after it.

H="Authorization: Bearer $KIOKO_API_KEY"
curl -s localhost:8765/v1/recall -H "$H" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"user_id": "asha", "session_id": "s1", "query": "What should I focus on this week?", "budget_tokens": 600}'
curl -s localhost:8765/v1/turns -H "$H" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"user_id": "asha", "session_id": "s1", "user_message": "My goal is to get line 3 OEE above 85% by December 31.",
       "assistant_message": "Noted."}'

The responses, abridged:

{"plan": {"intents": ["goals", "strategy"], ...}, "tokens": 74,
 "text": "<memory>\n...\nThe user's open goals:\n- Get line 3 OEE above 85% by December 31 (medium, 0%, due 2026-12-31)\n</memory>", ...}

{"results": [{"action": "added", "memory": {"memory_type": "goal",
              "content": "Goal: Get line 3 OEE above 85% by December 31.", ...}, ...}]}
Endpoint Purpose POST /v1/recall Everything the agent should know for a query, as a prompt-ready text plus the sections; hybrid, planned, within budget_tokens POST /v1/turns After a reply: store the exchange and learn from it (managed by the intelligence when it is on) POST /v1/manage What the intelligence decides for a turn (dry_run to preview) POST /v1/plan · POST /v1/maintain · GET /v1/intelligence Recall plans; reflect / pin / consolidate now; intelligence status and counters POST /v1/context · POST /v1/search · POST /v1/learn The lower-level read, search and extraction calls POST /v1/kinds/{kind}/{operation} · GET /v1/kinds Any typed operation, e.g. goals/add, decisions/supersede, graph/neighbors GET /v1/graph · POST /v1/consolidate · GET /v1/cache The knowledge graph, maintenance, cache statistics GET /v1/pins · POST/DELETE /v1/memories/{id}/pin Pinned (always-at-hand) memories POST /v1/memories · GET · GET/PATCH/DELETE /v1/memories/{id} · DELETE /v1/memories?user_id= Create, list, read, edit, delete; clear one user POST /v1/messages · GET /v1/sessions · GET /v1/sessions/{id}/messages · POST .../summarize · POST .../end · DELETE /v1/sessions/{id} Sessions and history GET /v1/events?after=<seq> · GET /v1/users · GET /v1/stats · GET /v1/info Activity log, users, counts, configuration GET /v1/health · GET /v1/openapi.json Liveness and the OpenAPI document (no key needed)

The OpenAPI document (kioko openapi --server-url https://memory.example.com > openapi.json) imports into Postman, Swagger UI, Azure API Management or a Power Platform custom connector.

From Python, kioko.connect("http://memory-service:8765") returns a RemoteMemory with the same API as a local memory: every kind, recall, manage, plan, pin .... It reads the API key from KIOKO_API_KEY. examples/rest_client.mjs is a Node client, and the cookbook has a Python one.

Security.

  • With KIOKO_API_KEY set, /v1 and /mcp require Authorization: Bearer <key> or X-API-Key.
  • Without a key, the server refuses to listen on a non-loopback address (unless you pass --insecure), and it checks Host and Origin headers.
  • One key grants access to every user's memories. Put a gateway in front for per-user authentication, and use HTTPS outside a private network.

docs.title: 9. MCP hosts
docs.text:
The same memory works as tools for Claude Desktop and Claude Code, VS Code with GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Copilot Studio and any other MCP client. The tools are:

  • get_memory_context, search_memory, list_memories, explore_entity;
  • save_memory, learn_from_conversation, manage_goal, record_decision, record_lesson, relate_entities;
  • update_memory, delete_memory.

The server decides whose memory the tools use, never the model.

{ "mcpServers": { "kioko": { "command": "kioko", "args": ["mcp", "--user", "asha", "--intelligence"] } } }

That is the stdio configuration for Claude Desktop or Cursor; memories go to ~/.kioko/memory.db. Over HTTP (VS Code .vscode/mcp.json, Copilot Studio), use https://<host>/mcp with the X-Kioko-User and Authorization headers. The README has the full configurations.

docs.title: 10. Look inside: the console
docs.text:
kioko ui --db plant-memory.db --intelligence --open        # http://127.0.0.1:8765
kioko ui --url http://memory-service:8765                   # manage a running service from your laptop

The console shows every user and session. You can chat with an agent and see what it recalled, injected and learned on each turn. You can browse, edit, pin and delete memories; inspect every kind, the graph and the working memory; preview the intelligence's decisions; plan and run recalls; and follow all activity live. Console explains how to reach it on a server (an SSH tunnel or --url) and how to keep it safe.

docs.title: 11. Keep it healthy
docs.text:
With intelligence on, maintenance runs by itself:

  • sessions are summarised;
  • recent episodes are reflected into insights;
  • hot memories are pinned;
  • sessions are wrapped up when a user moves on;
  • duplicates are merged and faded episodes forgotten.

For stores that several processes share, also run it nightly:

kioko maintain --store "$KIOKO_STORE_URL"           # every user: reflect, pin hot memories, consolidate

memory.maintain()                                    # the same from Python (POST /v1/maintain over REST)
memory.end_session("tue-shift", user_id="asha")      # when your app knows a session is over

Keep each context small with budget_tokens= on recall(). The default is 1200. Items that do not fit are listed in ctx.omitted, and the session summary is shortened rather than dropped.

docs.title: 12. Production checklist
docs.text:
• Embeddings. Use a semantic embedder (AzureOpenAIEmbedder, OpenAIEmbedder, AgnoEmbedder or a function). After switching, run memory.reembed().
  • Store. Use Postgres + pgvector or Qdrant for many processes and large memories, and SQLite for one machine. Back the database up like any other.
  • Intelligence. Offline is a good start. Add llm= for open-ended conversations and for languages other than English, because the rule-based extraction is English-only. Preview with dry_run, and watch the memory.managed events.
  • Secrets and PII. DropSecrets is on by default: passwords, API keys, tokens, private keys and card numbers are never stored, whoever proposes them. Add RedactPII to mask e-mails and phone numbers. Users can ask the assistant to forget things, and memory.clear(user_id=...) / DELETE /v1/memories?user_id= delete a user's data.
  • Service. Set KIOKO_API_KEY, terminate TLS in front, keep the console off the internet, and use --allowed-host behind a proxy.
  • Several workers. The context cache lives in each process for context_cache_ttl seconds (15). Lower it, or set it to 0 when several workers write the same users' memories.
  • Observability. Every write, recall and decision is an event. Subscribe with memory.subscribe(...), forward with WebhookSink, or poll GET /v1/events. memory.stats() and GET /v1/intelligence have counters.
  • Python 3.14. Annotations are evaluated lazily (PEP 649). attach() and @with_memory never force them.

docs.title: 14. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• "Nothing to remember (only questions or requests)." The gate skips turns that hold no information, such as questions and requests to the assistant. That is intended. Say it as a statement ("I'm based in Pune"), or use memory.add(...) / memory.facts.add(...).
  • A statement was not kept. Look at the report: memory.manage(text, user_id=..., dry_run=True).summary(). Unrecognised statements are kept only above min_importance. Use capture="all", add an extraction rule (RuleBasedExtractor(extra_rules=[Rule(...)])), or give the intelligence a model.
  • Recall misses something obvious. With the default lexical embedder, "car" does not match "automobile". Switch to a semantic embedder and run memory.reembed(). To see why each memory was or was not recalled, use the console's Recall tab (signals and scores).
  • pgvector: "permission denied to create extension vector". Have an administrator run CREATE EXTENSION vector; once in the database.
  • Qdrant: wrong vector size. A collection has one size. Use a new collection= after changing embedders.
  • The console says "Not self-managing". Start it with --intelligence, or open a memory built with kioko.intelligent(). Previews in the Intelligence tab work either way.

docs.title: Intelligent memory management
docs.text:
Kioko can manage its memory on its own. For every conversation turn it works out which kind of memory each piece of information belongs to and which operation fits: add a goal, record progress on it, replace an earlier decision, update a value that changed, forget something on request, or keep a ticket number in the session's scratchpad. Before every answer it decides which kinds to retrieve for the question. In the background it summarises, reflects, pins hot memories and tidies up.

Two modes:

  • Offline (default). Rules and algorithms decide. There is no model, no network and no cost, and the behaviour is deterministic.
  • With an LLM. One model call per turn decides every operation. Kioko's algorithms still skip trivial turns without calling the model, validate what the model proposes, and take over when the model fails.
import kioko

memory = kioko.intelligent()                                   # offline
memory = kioko.intelligent("sqlite:///memory.db", llm=ask)     # model-driven; ask(prompt) -> text

# Your agent loop does not change:
ctx = memory.recall(user_text, user_id="kumar", session_id="s1")          # planned retrieval
reply = my_llm(system=SYSTEM + "\n\n" + ctx.text, user=user_text)
memory.record_turn(user_text, reply, user_id="kumar", session_id="s1")    # managed writes + maintenance

Contents: Quick setup · What it decides · With an LLM · Planned retrieval · Maintenance · Efficiency, measured · Safety and control · Customising · Every surface · Research basis

docs.title: Quick setup
docs.text:
Where Offline With a model New memory in Python kioko.intelligent() kioko.intelligent(llm=ask) Existing MemoryLayer MemoryLayer(..., intelligence=True) MemoryLayer(..., intelligence=Intelligence(llm=ask)) Any store URL kioko.intelligent("postgresql://...") kioko.intelligent("qdrant://host:6333/memories", llm=ask) JSON config {"intelligence": "heuristic"} {"intelligence": {"type": "llm", "llm": {"$import": "my_app.models:ask"}}} Service / console kioko serve --intelligence · kioko ui --intelligence kioko serve --intelligence-llm my_app.models:ask

kioko.intelligent() takes anything kioko.connect() takes (memory://, sqlite:///path.db, a .db path, postgresql://..., qdrant://..., a config dict, an existing MemoryLayer). It also turns on the knowledge graph (auto_graph=True), and with llm= it writes session summaries with the model too. A service URL is rejected: a Kioko service runs its own intelligence (kioko serve --intelligence).

ask is any prompt -> text callable. An Agno Agent (.run) or a LangChain chat model (.invoke) works as well. With OpenAI or Azure OpenAI:

import os
from openai import OpenAI            # or: from openai import AzureOpenAI

client = OpenAI()

def ask(prompt: str) -> str:
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=os.environ["KIOKO_MODEL"], temperature=0, response_format={"type": "json_object"},
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return reply.choices[0].message.content

Once intelligence is on, the usual calls use it:

  • learn() and record_turn() route the turn. So do the Agno adapter, attach(), /v1/learn, /v1/turns and the MCP learn_from_conversation tool.
  • recall() plans the retrieval.
  • Maintenance runs after each turn when it is due.

The explicit calls are:

report = memory.manage("I'm 60% done with the Azure exam prep", user_id="kumar", dry_run=True)
print(report.summary())       # goal.progress "Pass the Azure AI Engineer exam by March 31" -> 60%
plan = memory.plan("How do I reset the safety relay?", user_id="kumar")
memory.end_session("s1", user_id="kumar")
memory.maintain(user_id="kumar")              # reflect + pin + consolidate, e.g. from a nightly job
memory.pin(memory_id); memory.unpin(memory_id); memory.pinned(user_id="kumar")

manage(), plan() and the maintenance calls also work on a layer built without intelligence=. They use the offline intelligence on demand, but learn() and recall() keep their plain behaviour.
