Every decision comes back as a MemoryOp in a ManageReport. Each op has the operation, a readable description, the reason, the importance, a confidence and a status (planned in a dry run, then applied, skipped or failed):

report = memory.manage("I think maybe it's raining.", user_id="kumar")
report.ops[0].status, report.ops[0].error
# ('skipped', 'importance 0.37 < 0.4')
report.to_dict()          # JSON for logs, the REST API and the console

docs.title: The operations
docs.text:
Kind Actions profile set, remove fact add, update, delete, verify preference add, update, delete instruction add, update, delete knowledge (semantic) add, update, delete episode add, delete goal add, update, progress, complete, drop, delete decision add, supersede, outcome, delete procedure add, outcome, delete skill outcome strategy add, outcome, delete relation (graph) add, remove working set, remove, promote insight (reflection) add memory (any kind) update, delete, pin, unpin

OpExecutor applies an operation through the typed manager of its kind. So every operation goes through the same processors as any write (for example DropSecrets), and gets the same de-duplication, version history and events.

docs.title: How the offline router decides
docs.text:
For each turn, HeuristicRouter:

  1. Gate. It skips turns with nothing to remember: greetings, thanks, acknowledgements, and turns made only of questions or requests to the assistant ("Can you summarize this?"). A "remember ..." or a standing instruction is never gated. This is the cheap "sensory" filter that LightMem puts in front of memory processing.
  2. Feedback. If the user says a suggestion worked or failed ("that fixed it", "still broken"), the outcome is credited to the procedure, skill or lesson that the last recall() of this session gave the agent. When several were given, it picks the one the agent's reply echoes most. One "thanks, that worked" counts once. A fix that worked is also linked to the problem of the session it solved (resolves), and the links among what the agent was given are strengthened, so the next time the problem comes up recall brings the fix.
  3. State changes, per clause. "Finished / passed / shipped X", "N% done with X", "halfway through X" and "gave up on X" are matched against the user's open goals, but only when X is the goal itself and not a step towards it: "I finished the downtime analysis for line 2" or "I finished the prep for the Azure exam" is recorded as an episode and leaves the goal open (progress on a piece, "60% done with the exam prep", does count as progress). "Switched from A to B" and "B instead of A" are matched against current decisions. "I moved from A to B" changes the location only when A and B can be places, not a tool or platform, and A is the known location (or, when none is known, not the choice of a current decision). "Forget ..." and "don't remember ..." delete the user's own memories that contain at least 75% of the words, or the named profile slot ("forget my phone number"). "Delete", "remove" and "clear" count only when they point at the assistant's memory ("delete my address from your memory", "remove everything you know about X", "clear all memories about the PLC"); "delete the staging database" and "clear the memory on the PLC" are about the user's work, and are left alone.
  4. Extraction. The rule-based extractor recognises profile facts, preferences, instructions, goals, decisions, procedures, lessons and dated episodes. A restated goal ("my goal is to pass the Azure exam") is recognised as an open goal and not added twice. A fact that differs only in numbers ("two kids" → "three kids") becomes an update. A preference about how to answer ("I prefer short answers") becomes a standing instruction, so it applies to every turn and not only when it happens to be relevant.
  5. Classification of the rest. The informative clauses that no rule recognised are classified:
    • first-person present → fact;
    • past tense, a time cue or an ongoing activity → episode;
    • impersonal general statements → knowledge.

They are kept only if their importance reaches min_importance (0.4). Episodes fade away again in consolidation if they never turn out to matter. 6. Working memory. With a session_id, the current task ("I'm debugging ...") and identifiers (ticket and work-order numbers, error codes, links, file paths) go to the session's scratchpad. The task is not also stored as a fact. 7. Graph. With auto_graph, relations between named entities are added. Every memory the turn writes is also linked to related memories (a decision serves a goal, a fix resolves an incident); the report lists them as linked: .... The algorithm is in Graph memory.

Importance starts from the kind (instruction 0.8, goal and decision 0.75, procedure 0.7, fact 0.6, knowledge 0.55, episode 0.45 ...) and is then adjusted:

  • explicit cues ("remember", "important", "must") +0.2;
  • emotion or high stakes ("outage", "safety", "deadline", "allergic") +0.1;
  • specific details (numbers, names) +0.04 each, up to three;
  • hedging or temporariness ("maybe", "for now") −0.15;
  • very short statements −0.08.

It is a model-free stand-in for the Generative Agents poignancy score.

Matching a mention to a goal or decision needs either two shared content words covering at least half of the mention, or every word of a one- or two-word mention. Generic words ("goal", "task", "project", "prep") never match on their own.

capture= chooses how much is kept: "rules" keeps only what rules and detectors recognise, "selective" (the default) adds the classification step, and "all" keeps every informative statement.

docs.title: With an LLM
docs.text:
LLMRouter makes one call per turn. The prompt (see kioko.intelligence.DEFAULT_MANAGE_PROMPT) shows the model:

  • the user's memories related to the turn, as refs m1 ... m10 (Mem0 also shows its update step the ten most similar memories);
  • open goals g1 ... and current decisions d1 ...;
  • the procedures, skills and lessons the agent was given for this turn p1 ...;
  • the session's working memory and today's date;
  • the conversation turn.

The model answers with the operations:

{"operations": [
  {"op": "goal.progress", "target": "g1", "progress": 0.6, "reason": "12 of the 20 percentage points"},
  {"op": "decision.add", "title": "Dashboard tool for line 3", "chosen": "Grafana",
   "options": ["Grafana", "Power BI"], "rationale": "better alerting"}
]}

Kioko then:

  • validates: the kind and action must be in OPERATIONS, the required fields must be present, and a target must be one of the refs the model was shown. A made-up id is skipped, so a model can never reach memories it was not shown, or another user's;
  • applies through the same executor as the offline router. DropSecrets still drops credentials the model tries to store, and ownership is checked again;
  • gates: small talk and pure questions never reach the model. In the recipe below, 4 of 14 turns needed a call;
  • falls back: when the call fails or returns nothing parseable, the offline router routes the turn. The report shows router="llm->heuristic" and the error.

This output is from examples/cookbook/21_llm_intelligence.py, using a scripted stand-in model:

you > Downtime is already down 12%.
      [llm, 1 LLM call(s)]
      goal.progress "Cut unplanned downtime on line 3 by 20%" -> 60%

you > My API key is sk-EXAMPLE-not-a-real-key-000, keep it for later.
      [llm, 1 LLM call(s)]
      fact.add "User's API key is sk-EXAMPLE-not-a-real-key-000"   <- skipped: rejected by a processor (for example it looked like a secret)

you > thanks!
      [llm, 0 LLM call(s)]
      skipped before calling the model: small talk

you > I prefer bullet points over long paragraphs.
      [llm->heuristic, 1 LLM call(s)]
      instruction.add "User prefers bullet points over long paragraphs."
      the model failed (ValueError: no operations JSON found in the model output); the offline router decided instead

With a model, reflection also uses it. Recent episodes (e1 ...) go to the model, which returns higher-level insights with their evidence. They are stored as facts, preferences, knowledge or lessons with metadata.reflection = True and the evidence ids.

To change the wording, pass your own prompt: LLMRouter(ask, prompt_template=...). It must keep the {related}, {goals}, {decisions}, {served}, {working}, {today} and {conversation} placeholders.

docs.title: Planned retrieval (the read path)
docs.text:
QueryPlanner reads the intent of the query offline and returns a RecallPlan: the context sections to build and a cap for each. recall() follows it whenever the layer has intelligence, or when you pass plan="auto". ctx.plan shows the plan it followed.

Intent Example What the plan does howto "How do I reset the safety relay?" procedures 3, lessons 3, skills 2; fewer facts, decisions, graph decision "Why did we choose pgvector?" decision log 5, graph 6; no skills; falls back to the newest decisions goals "What should I focus on next?" every open goal, the working memory, decisions 2 temporal "When did line 3 stop last week?" 10 relevant items (episodes); recency counts in hybrid search personal "What do you know about me?" profile up to 30 slots, 8 personal facts; no procedures, skills, lessons relational "Who is Krutika?", or any entity the graph knows graph up to 15 relations knowledge "What is the default OPC UA port?" knowledge 6, graph 8 skills "Do we have a prompt template for alarm logs?" skills 4, procedures 2 strategy "What's the best way to debug a drive fault?" lessons 4, decisions 2 smalltalk / feedback "thanks!", "that worked" only the stable part: instructions, profile, goals, pinned, working; no retrieval (none) anything else every kind with the default caps

A query can have several intents. Then the largest cap wins, and a section is dropped only if no intent needs it. Entities that the user's knowledge graph knows add the relational intent. Options you pass to recall() explicitly win over the plan: recall(q, plan="auto", section_limits={"procedures": 0}).

A decision question often shares no word with the decision itself: "which database did we settle on?" against "Decision: use Qdrant because it is managed". With a semantic embedder the search still finds it; with the offline hashing embedder it would not. So the plan sets fill_recent=["decisions"]: when the search finds no decision, the section is filled with the newest decisions that are still in force (superseded ones are left out). You can ask for the same thing yourself with context(q, fill_recent=["decisions"]), or for procedures, skills and strategies.

The plan also sets links, how many memories recall brings in through the memory graph: 6 for relational questions, 4 for decisions and goals, 3 for how-tos and general questions, none for small talk (Graph memory, section 6).

plan = memory.plan("How do I reset the safety relay?", user_id="kumar")
plan.intents, plan.reason, plan.section_limits
# (['howto'], 'a how-to question: procedures, skills and lessons first',
#  {'procedures': 3, 'skills': 2, 'strategies': 3, 'knowledge': 3, 'decisions': 1, 'graph': 4})
memory.recall(q, user_id="kumar", plan=False)      # every kind, default caps
memory.recall(q, user_id="kumar", plan=plan)       # a plan you built or edited

This is the routing idea of Adaptive-RAG (sending a query to no, single-step or multi-step retrieval) applied to memory kinds. LLMPlanner(llm) lets a model name the intents instead. That costs one small extra call per query, so it is off by default (Intelligence(llm=..., plan_with_llm=True) turns it on).

docs.title: Maintenance (sleep-time)
docs.text:
MaintenanceScheduler keeps a few counters per user and runs what is due after each turn:

Task When (default) What it does Idea from summarise session every 10 turns of a session folds older turns into the session's rolling summary MemGPT recursive summaries reflect the new memories' importance adds up to 2.5 and at least 3 new episodes arrived with a model: insights with evidence. Offline: a "recurring theme" memory per subject ("line 3", "E-217", "OPC UA") or word that comes up in 3 or more recent episodes, updated in place; a word that only appears inside a subject gives way to it Generative Agents reflection pin hot memories every 10 turns pins memories with heat ≥ 5 and keeps at most 5 automatic pins per user (the coldest give way); unpins them below 3. Heat = (times recalled + times re-mentioned), halved every 28 days without use, + recency (half-life 7 days). Manual pins are never touched MemoryOS heat promotion (τ = 5); MemOS plaintext → activation tend the memory graph every 25 turns links memories that were never linked, removes faded and dangling links, and with a model reviews the 12 most recent automatic links (keep, retype or drop) in one call A-MEM link generation and memory evolution end session the user starts a new session, or end_session() lasting scratchpad slots (result, root cause, fix, decision ...) and the task become one episode for the session; summarises the conversation; an explicit call also clears the scratchpad MemGPT working context → archival consolidate every 200 applied operations expires, folds old episodes into summaries, merges duplicates, forgets faded episodes survey operations: consolidation, forgetting

Pinned memories are always in the context, in a pinned section ("Keep in mind (frequently needed)") right after the goals. That keeps the things a user needs again and again at hand without a search. They are also part of the stable, cacheable prefix that memory.kv builds for provider prompt caches. Being shown in the pinned section does not count as a use. Only when a query retrieves a pinned memory on its own does it count, so a pin that is no longer needed cools down and is removed. Pin and unpin by hand with memory.pin(id) and memory.unpin(id), or the Pin button in the console.

Maintenance never raises into the agent's turn. With Intelligence(background=True) the due tasks run on one worker thread. For a nightly job:

kioko maintain --db memory.db                        # every user: reflect, pin, consolidate
kioko maintain --store postgresql://... --user kumar --tasks reflect,pin

or memory.maintain() / POST /v1/maintain. Thresholds are constructor options: Intelligence(summarize_every=20, reflect_after=5, pin_threshold=8, max_pinned=3, consolidate_every=500). Use 0 or None to turn a task off, and scheduler=False to turn all of them off.

docs.title: Efficiency, measured
docs.text:
examples/cookbook/22_efficiency.py builds a realistic memory: a profile, rules, goals, 4 decisions, 4 procedures, lessons, 40 facts, 30 episodes and 20 knowledge items. It then measures three things.

Tokens per recall, with every kind at default caps and with the intent-based plan, no budget. The recipe uses a stand-in for a semantic embedding model: unrelated texts keep a baseline similarity, so every memory competes for a place in the context.

query                                    every kind  planned  intents
How do I reset the safety relay?                459      366  howto
Why did we choose pgvector?                     467      363  decision
What are my goals?                              348      235  goals
What do you know about me?                      238      238  personal
thanks!                                         402      123  smalltalk
When did line 3 stop for a jam?                 297      304  temporal
Which device does station 12 use?               395      395  general
What is the port of OPC UA endpoint 3?          354      317  knowledge
total                                          2960     2341  -> 21% fewer tokens

Planning saves most where a question needs only part of the memory: small talk, goals and how-tos. A temporal question gets slightly more, because the plan asks for more episodes. Numbers vary a little between runs, because recency and access counts take part in the ranking. With the default lexical embedder, retrieval is already narrow, so the plan mostly changes what is retrieved rather than how much.

Model calls the gate avoids, in LLM mode, over a 14-turn conversation:

gate: 4 model calls for 14 turns (10 skipped as small talk, questions or requests)

What rides in the cacheable prefix. After five differently worded questions about the PLC subnet, the scheduler pins that fact. From then on it is part of the stable prefix, byte-identical from turn to turn:

stable prefix: 33 tokens (profile, pinned); byte-identical next turn: True
About the user:
- User's name is Kumar.

Keep in mind (frequently needed):
- The plant's PLC network uses the 10.20.0.0/16 subnet

docs.title: Safety and control
docs.text:
• Preview first. manage(..., dry_run=True), kioko manage ... --dry-run and the console's Preview decisions button decide without writing anything.
  • Everything is reported. Every managed turn emits a memory.managed event with the operations, the router, model calls and maintenance. The console's Activity tab has an Intelligence filter, and webhooks receive the event too. memory.intelligence.stats() counts turns, gated turns, model calls, fallbacks, operations and plans.
  • Scope is enforced. Updates and deletes only reach memories of the turn's user (and agent). Outcome feedback may also reach agent-level procedures and skills that the user's context used. Knowledge learned from a conversation is stored in the user's own scope, never in the shared knowledge base.
  • Secrets are dropped, whichever router proposed them.
  • Forgetting is a real delete of the user's own memories. A request that matches nothing is reported as skipped. "Forget it" and "forget everything" are never acted on: wiping everything stays an explicit API call.
  • Interleaved sessions. A session switch only wraps the old session up and keeps its scratchpad. The session episode is keyed, so wrapping a session up again updates it.

docs.title: Customising
docs.text:
from kioko import Intelligence, HeuristicRouter, LLMRouter, MaintenanceScheduler, MemoryLayer, QueryPlanner

brain = Intelligence(
    router=HeuristicRouter(capture="rules", min_importance=0.5, working=True, feedback=True),
    planner=QueryPlanner(use_graph=True),
    scheduler=MaintenanceScheduler(summarize_every=20, pin_threshold=8, background=True),
)
memory = MemoryLayer.sqlite("memory.db", intelligence=brain)

Each part is a protocol, so you can plug in your own:

  • a router has route(memory, turn) -> RouteResult. turn.texts("user"), turn.session_id and turn.served hold the inputs; return MemoryOps;
  • a planner has plan(memory, query, *, user_id, agent_id, session_id, limit) -> RecallPlan;
  • a scheduler has after_turn(memory, report, *, user_id, agent_id, session_id) -> list (and optionally end_session, reflect, run);
  • an object with manage(memory, messages, ...) can replace the whole Intelligence: MemoryLayer(intelligence=my_brain).

To combine your own rules with the model, set LLMRouter(ask, fallback=HeuristicRouter(...)). To add patterns the offline router should know, pass an extractor: HeuristicRouter(extractor=RuleBasedExtractor(extra_rules=[...])).

docs.title: Research basis
docs.text:
Kioko's intelligence borrows from published memory systems. Each item below lists what it took. The mechanisms were checked against the primary sources.

  • Mem0, Chhikara et al. 2025, arXiv:2504.19413. Its update phase asks an LLM to choose ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or NOOP for each new fact against the 10 most similar memories, through a tool call. Kioko's LLM router does the same in one call for the whole turn, with typed operations for every kind and the similar memories shown as refs.
  • MIRIX, Wang & Chen 2025, arXiv:2507.07957. A Meta Memory Manager routes input to per-type managers for core, episodic, semantic, procedural, resource and vault memory. Kioko's router plays that role over its kinds, and recall's planner is a cheap form of their "active retrieval".
  • Memory-R1, Yan et al. 2025, arXiv:2508.19828. A memory manager trained with RL to choose ADD, UPDATE, DELETE or NOOP. It confirms the operation set Kioko validates against.
  • Generative Agents, Park et al. 2023, arXiv:2304.03442. Importance scored 1–10 at creation, reflection triggered when recent importance adds up past 150, and retrieval by recency + importance + relevance. Kioko uses a model-free importance score on a 0–1 scale and the same summed-importance reflection trigger.
  • A-MEM, Xu et al. 2025, arXiv:2502.12110. Notes with keywords, tags and links to similar notes (an LLM decides which links to create among the most similar notes), and "memory evolution" that can update the retrieved neighbours. Kioko's memory graph links every new memory at write time with an algorithmic judge and lets a model review the links (Graph memory).
  • LightMem, Fang et al. 2025, arXiv:2510.18866. Sensory pre-compression, topic-aware short-term summaries, and long-term updates done offline ("sleep time"). Kioko's gate is the sensory filter, and the scheduler and maintain() do the offline work.
  • MemOS, Li et al. 2025, arXiv:2505.22101 and arXiv:2507.03724. A scheduler moves frequently used plaintext memory into activation (KV-cache) memory and stable knowledge into parameters. Pinning hot memories into the cacheable prefix, and memory.parametric, follow that path.
  • MemoryOS, Kang et al. 2025, arXiv:2506.06326. Promotion by heat = visits + interaction length + recency, with threshold τ = 5. Kioko's pin heat is the same sum, with recalls, re-mentions and a 7-day half-life, and the default threshold of 5. Unlike MemoryOS, the counts fade (halved every 28 days without use), so a pin that stops being used cools down and is released.
  • MemGPT, Packer et al. 2023, arXiv:2310.08560. Memory pressure, evicting old messages and recursive summaries. These are Kioko's rolling session summaries and session wrap-up.
  • Letta sleep-time agents (blog), with the related paper Lin et al. 2025, arXiv:2504.13171. A background agent reorganises memory while the main agent is idle. This is background=True and maintain().
  • LangMem (memory manager docs, delayed processing). Memory managers with insert, update and delete, and a debounced background executor.
  • Adaptive-RAG, Jeong et al. 2024, arXiv:2403.14403. A classifier routes each query to no, single-step or multi-step retrieval. Kioko's planner routes queries to memory kinds, and small talk to no retrieval.
  • Survey, Du et al. 2025, arXiv:2505.00675 ("Rethinking Memory in AI"; v3 is titled "Rethinking Memory in LLM based Agents"). Its memory operations are consolidation, indexing, updating, forgetting, retrieval and condensation (called compression in v1). Each one has a counterpart above.

docs.title: MCP server
docs.text:
The tools: get_memory_context (hybrid, planned recall), search_memory, list_memories, explore_entity, explore_memories (how memories connect), save_memory, learn_from_conversation, manage_goal, record_decision, record_lesson, relate_entities, update_memory and delete_memory. Start the server with --intelligence and learn_from_conversation also updates goals and decisions, keeps task details in working memory and forgets on request. Read-only tools are annotated, and --read-only exposes only those. The user whose memory the tools use is set by the server (--user, or the X-Kioko-User header over HTTP). The model can never choose it, so a prompt injection can't reach another user's memories. Protocol revisions 2024-11-05 to 2025-11-25 are supported.

Desktop hosts (stdio). For Claude Desktop (claude_desktop_config.json), Cursor (~/.cursor/mcp.json) and similar hosts:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "kioko": { "command": "kioko", "args": ["mcp", "--user", "kumar"] }
  }
}

With no --db, memories go to ~/.kioko/memory.db. Use --url http://memory-service:8765 (plus KIOKO_API_KEY in env) to share a central service. For Claude Code: claude mcp add kioko -- kioko mcp --user kumar.

VS Code / GitHub Copilot (HTTP), in .vscode/mcp.json:

{
  "servers": {
    "kioko": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "http://localhost:8765/mcp",
      "headers": { "X-Kioko-User": "kumar", "Authorization": "Bearer ${input:kioko-key}" }
    }
  },
  "inputs": [{ "type": "promptString", "id": "kioko-key", "description": "Kioko API key", "password": true }]
}

Copilot Studio and other remote clients. Use the Streamable HTTP endpoint https://<your-host>/mcp, with API-key authentication as Authorization: Bearer <key> or X-API-Key, served by kioko serve behind HTTPS. The server answers with JSON, keeps no sessions, and returns 405 to GET.

docs.title: Memory types
docs.text:
Kioko has fifteen kinds of memory. Each one is an ordinary memory record: a memory_type, structured metadata and, where it makes sense, a slot key. That has three consequences:

  • every store supports every kind (in-process, SQLite, Postgres + pgvector, Qdrant, a remote service);
  • every kind gets the same pipeline: secret filtering, de-duplication, version history, events, and the console's views;
  • one recall() can search every kind together.

Each kind has a typed manager on the memory object (memory.goals, memory.graph, memory.working(session) ...). The managers use only the public memory API, so the same code runs on a local MemoryLayer and on a RemoteMemory client.

# Kind Accessor Remembers In the context Recipe 1 Profile memory.profile who the user is, one value per slot always, About the user 01 2 Factual memory.facts facts and preferences, with confidence when relevant 02 3 Semantic memory.semantic domain knowledge, shared or personal when relevant, Background knowledge 03 4 Episodic memory.episodes events with when / where / who / outcome when relevant 04 5 Working memory.working(session) the current task's scratchpad always for the session 05 6 Conversational memory.conversation(session) rolling summary + recent turns the session summary 06 7 Goal memory.goals objectives, progress, due dates always, Open goals 07 8 Procedural memory.procedures how-tos with versioned steps; standing rules matching procedures; rules always 08 9 Skill memory.skills reusable prompts, tools, code, with a track record matching skills 09 10 Strategy memory.strategies what worked for which kind of task matching lessons 10 11 Decision memory.decisions decisions with rationale and history matching decisions 11 12 Graph memory.graph entities and relations, with time relations around named entities 12 13 KV cache memory.kv cacheable prompt prefix, embedding and context caches the stable prefix 13 14 Parametric memory.parametric the bridge to fine-tuned weights consolidated memories left out 14 15 Hybrid memory.recall() / memory.hybrid one retrieval over every kind and representation the whole block 15

On top of the kinds sit pinned memories: hot memories in a Keep in mind section that always rides in the cacheable prefix (see intelligence). They are not a kind of their own, and any fact, knowledge item, procedure, skill, lesson or decision can be pinned.

You rarely need to call the managers yourself. memory.learn() / record_turn() fill the kinds from conversation, and the intelligence also updates them: progress on goals, superseded decisions, outcomes of procedures. The APIs below are for when your code knows something directly, or for tools your agent calls.

All examples use user = "kumar" and from kioko import MemoryLayer; memory = MemoryLayer().

docs.title: 1. Profile memory
docs.text:
Stable facts about who the user is: name, location, employer, role, languages, manager, time zone. Each slot holds one value. A new value replaces the old one, and the old one stays in the record's history. Profile slots are ordinary memories keyed profile.<slot>. The rule extractor writes the same keys, so "I moved to Hyderabad" from a conversation updates the same slot.

memory.profile.set("location", "Pune", user_id=user)
memory.profile.set("location", "Bengaluru", user_id=user)            # updated, not duplicated
memory.profile.get(user_id=user)                  # {'location': 'Bengaluru'}
memory.profile.history("location", user_id=user)  # previous values with timestamps
memory.profile.remove("phone_number", user_id=user)

Context: always included (About the user), and part of the cacheable prefix.

docs.title: 2. Factual memory
docs.text:
Durable statements about the user or their world ("User's team has 6 engineers") and preferences ("User prefers concise answers").

  • A fact can carry a slot key; a new value for the key updates it.
  • It can carry a confidence and be marked verified.
  • Contradictions supersede automatically: "doesn't like hiking anymore" replaces "likes hiking".
  • Near-duplicates reinforce the existing memory instead of adding one.
memory.facts.add("User's manager is Krutika", key="work.manager", user_id=user, confidence=0.9)
memory.facts.add("User prefers metric units", preference=True, user_id=user)
memory.facts.verify(record, user_id=user)
memory.facts.search("units", user_id=user)

Context: the Relevant memories section, ranked by the query.

docs.title: 3. Semantic memory
docs.text:
General or domain knowledge: product facts, policies, definitions, runbooks. It is not about a user. By default it lives in the shared namespace (@shared), which every user's context can draw on. Pass user_id= to keep knowledge personal, or namespace= for a team or product scope. ingest() splits a document into searchable chunks. Re-ingesting the same source updates the chunks instead of duplicating them.

memory.semantic.add("OPC UA servers listen on TCP port 4840 by default", topic="iiot")      # shared
memory.semantic.ingest(open("runbook.md").read(), source="runbook-v3", topic="operations")
memory.semantic.search("default OPC UA port", user_id=user)      # the user's own + shared knowledge
memory.semantic.forget_source("runbook-v2")

Context: Background knowledge, from the user's own knowledge and the shared base. Knowledge that the intelligence learns from a conversation stays in the user's own scope.

docs.title: 4. Episodic memory
docs.text:
What happened, when, where, with whom and how it ended. These are time-stamped experiences. Repeated events are separate episodes (two gym visits are two episodes), so episodes are never de-duplicated. As they age, consolidate() folds clusters of similar old episodes into summary memories. Faded episodes are forgotten: the score is importance × recency × how often they were recalled.

memory.episodes.record("Presented the predictive-maintenance demo to the plant team", user_id=user,
                       when="2026-10-20", where="Pune plant", who=["Krutika"], outcome="approved for a pilot")
memory.episodes.timeline(user_id=user, since="2026-10-01")
memory.episodes.recent(user_id=user, days=7)
memory.episodes.consolidate(user_id=user, older_than_days=30)

Context: Relevant memories. For "when did ..." questions the planner asks for more of them and hybrid recall weighs recency.

docs.title: 5. Working memory
docs.text:
The scratchpad for the task at hand: the current task, intermediate results, ticket numbers, open questions.

  • It is session-scoped.
  • It is small: capacity=10 items; the least recently updated item is evicted first.
  • It expires: ttl_seconds defaults to 6 hours.
  • It is never embedded, so writing it costs nothing.

It never pollutes long-term memory unless an item is promoted.

wm = memory.working("shift-1", user_id=user)
wm.set("task", "Fix the E-217 fault on line 3")
wm.set("ticket", "INC-4521")
wm.snapshot()                          # {'task': ..., 'ticket': ...}
wm.promote("root_cause", memory_type="fact")      # keep a conclusion long-term
memory.end_session("shift-1", user_id=user)       # lasting slots -> an episode, then cleared

Context: always included for the session (Current task notes). The intelligence fills it from what the user says: the task, ticket and work-order numbers, error codes, links and file paths.

docs.title: 6. Conversational memory
docs.text:
The dialogue of one session, kept at constant size however long it gets: the last keep_last turns verbatim, and everything older folded into a rolling summary (session:<id>:summary) once more than summarize_after messages are not yet covered. The summary is written by the configured summarizer: extractive offline, or LLMSummarizer(llm).

chat = memory.conversation("s1", user_id=user, keep_last=6, summarize_after=20)
chat.add_turn("How do I reset the relay?", "Switch off the breaker, then ...")
chat.as_messages(system="You are a plant support agent.")      # summary + recent turns, ready for an LLM
chat.context(max_tokens=600)

Context: Earlier in this session (the summary). history_turns= adds the last turns verbatim.

docs.title: 7. Goal memory
docs.text:
What the user, or the agent, is working towards. A goal has:

  • a status: active, blocked, paused, done or dropped;
  • a priority: low, medium, high or critical;
  • progress from 0 to 1;
  • an optional due date, success criteria, a reason, and a parent for sub-goals;
  • an update trail.

Open goals are always in the agent's view, most important first, then the soonest due. Overdue goals are flagged.

goal = memory.goals.add("Ship Kioko 1.0", user_id=user, priority="high", due="2026-12-15",
                        criteria="published and installable")
memory.goals.add("Write the cookbook", user_id=user, parent=goal)
memory.goals.update(goal, user_id=user, progress=0.6, note="all kinds done")
memory.goals.complete(goal, user_id=user)
memory.goals.tree(user_id=user)

Context: always included (The user's open goals), and part of the cacheable prefix. The intelligence records progress ("I'm 60% done with ..."), completion ("I shipped ...") and dropped goals ("I gave up on ...") from conversation.

docs.title: 8. Procedural memory
docs.text:
How to do things. A procedure has named, ordered steps, an optional when to use, preconditions and tools. Changing the steps creates a new version, and the old text stays in history. It also keeps a success and failure record, so find() prefers procedures that work. Standing rules ("Always cite the ticket number") are procedural memory at the prompt level: add_rule() stores them as instructions that are always applied.

memory.procedures.add("Reset the safety relay", user_id=user, when_to_use="the relay trips",
                      steps=["Switch off the main breaker", "Press reset for 5 seconds", "Switch the breaker on"])
memory.procedures.find("the relay tripped again", user_id=user)
memory.procedures.record_outcome("Reset the safety relay", success=True, user_id=user)
memory.procedures.add_rule("Always cite the ticket number", user_id=user)

Context: matching procedures in Procedures that may apply; rules in Instructions. When the user says "that worked" or "still broken", the intelligence credits the outcome to the procedure the agent just used.

docs.title: 9. Skill memory
docs.text:
Reusable capabilities: prompts, tools, code and workflows (kind="prompt" | "tool" | "code" | "workflow"). Each skill has a description, a body, inputs and a usage record (successes, failures, latency). find() ranks by relevance × reliability. Reliability is the Wilson lower bound of the success rate, so 3 successes out of 3 rank below 90 out of 100.

memory.skills.add("summarize alarm log", description="Top recurring faults from a PLC alarm log",
                  body="Summarize these alarms by fault code and count: {alarms}", user_id=user)
skill, score = memory.skills.find("summarise the alarms from line 3", user_id=user)[0]
memory.skills.render_prompt(skill, user_id=user, alarms="E-217 x12, E-301 x4")
memory.skills.record_use(skill, success=True, latency_ms=820, user_id=user)

Context: Skills you can use.

docs.title: 10. Strategy memory
docs.text:
Lessons about what works for which kind of task, in the style of Reflexion and ExpeL. Each reflect(task_type, approach, outcome) updates the approach's track record (success, partial, failure) and its lessons. recommend() returns approaches that worked, and avoid() returns those that mostly failed.

memory.strategies.reflect("debugging drives", "check the encoder cable first", "success", user_id=user)
memory.strategies.reflect("debugging drives", "replace the drive", "failure", user_id=user,
                          lesson="expensive and rarely the cause")
memory.strategies.recommend("drive fault on line 3", user_id=user)
memory.strategies.avoid("drive fault on line 3", user_id=user)

Context: Lessons from earlier attempts. "Lesson learned: ..." in conversation becomes a strategy.

docs.title: 11. Decision memory
docs.text:
A decision log in the style of architecture decision records. Each decision has a title (the question), the chosen option, the options considered, the rationale, the context, a status (proposed, accepted, superseded or reverted), an outcome and a review date. A new decision on the same question supersedes the old one, and the two are linked, so chain() shows how a decision evolved and a title always resolves to the current decision.

memory.decisions.record("Vector store", chosen="Qdrant", options=["Qdrant", "pgvector"],
                        rationale="fast to set up", user_id=user)
memory.decisions.supersede("Vector store", chosen="pgvector", rationale="we already run Postgres", user_id=user)
[d.chosen for d in memory.decisions.chain("Vector store", user_id=user)]      # ['Qdrant', 'pgvector']
memory.decisions.set_outcome("Vector store", "query latency halved", user_id=user)

Context: current decisions in Earlier decisions; superseded ones are left out. The intelligence turns "we switched from Qdrant to pgvector because ..." into a supersede.

docs.title: 12. Graph memory
docs.text:
A temporal knowledge graph of entities (people, teams, systems, places) and relations (subject -predicate-> object).

  • Single-valued predicates (lives_in, works_at, reports_to, has_manager ...) replace their old object and keep it as history with the period it was valid.
  • Entities can have types and aliases.
  • neighbors(), path() and about() answer multi-hop questions.
  • With auto_graph=True (on by default in kioko.intelligent()), relations are extracted from conversation.
memory.graph.add("Kumar", "reports_to", "Krutika", user_id=user)
memory.graph.add("Krutika", "leads", "AI & IIoT architecture", user_id=user)
memory.graph.add_entity("Krutika", type="person", aliases=["KK"], user_id=user)
memory.graph.about("Krutika", user_id=user)
memory.graph.path("Kumar", "AI & IIoT architecture", user_id=user)
memory.graph.relations(user_id=user, at="2026-01-01")     # the graph as it was on a date

Context: Known relationships around the entities the query names. Hybrid recall also uses graph mentions as a ranking signal.

Memory links: the second layer. Graph memory also connects the memories themselves. Each new memory is linked to the memories it is related to, with a type and the evidence: a decision serves a goal, a lesson refines a procedure, a fix resolves an incident, an insight is derived from its episodes. The evidence is shared entities and rare words, meaning, a relation in the entity graph above ("Kioko uses pgvector" connects a pgvector decision to a Kioko goal), and the same session. Recall follows the links (spreading activation) and the context gains a How these memories connect section. The full algorithm, with formulas and worked examples, is in Graph memory.

memory.graph.links(memory_id)                  # [MemoryLink]: decision "use pgvector" serves goal "Ship Kioko"
memory.graph.related(memory_id, depth=2)       # what is connected, best first, with the chain of links
memory.graph.explain(a, b)                     # the evidence, and whether the algorithm links them
memory.graph.link(a, b, type="resolves")       # by hand (never fades)
memory.graph.connect(user_id=user)             # link memories written before linking was on

Context: How these memories connect, the links among the memories in the block, plus up to links memories brought in by their links (the recall plan sets how many).

docs.title: 13. KV-cache memory
docs.text:
Memory that saves compute rather than storing facts.

  1. Prompt-prefix caching. memory.kv lays a request out with the stable part first: instructions, profile, goals and pinned memories, sorted deterministically, so the prefix is byte-identical from turn to turn. Provider prompt caches can then serve it. It has helpers for Anthropic (a cache_control breakpoint, optional 1-hour ttl) and OpenAI (stable system message first, prompt_cache_key). The same layout works with vLLM's prefix caching or llama.cpp's cache_prompt.
  2. An embedding cache. Each distinct text is embedded once (embedding_cache=4096).
  3. A context cache. An identical context() call within context_cache_ttl seconds (15) is served from memory, unless a write changed the user's memories in between.
prefix = memory.kv.prefix(user_id=user)               # .text .hash .tokens .reused .sections
system = memory.kv.anthropic_system("Which PLCs do we use?", user_id=user, base_system=SYSTEM, ttl="1h")
messages = memory.kv.openai_messages("Which PLCs do we use?", user_id=user, base_system=SYSTEM)
memory.kv.stats()                                      # prefix reuse, cache hit rates

docs.title: 14. Parametric memory
docs.text:
The bridge to model weights. Stable, much-used memories (facts, preferences, instructions, procedures, skills, decisions, knowledge) can be exported as a fine-tuning dataset. Once a model has learned them, they are marked as consolidated into it. context(model=...) then stops spending tokens on them. probe() checks with the model which memories it really answers correctly.

rows = memory.parametric.export_dataset("train.jsonl", user_id=user, format="openai-chat")
memory.parametric.register_model("ft:plant-assistant-v1", base_model="<base model>", kind="lora", user_id=user)
memory.parametric.mark_consolidated(memory.parametric.candidates(user_id=user), model="ft:plant-assistant-v1")
ctx = memory.recall("What controllers does line 3 use?", user_id=user, model="ft:plant-assistant-v1")

docs.title: 15. Hybrid memory
docs.text:
One retrieval over every kind and every representation. recall() ranks candidates four ways:

  • dense similarity of embeddings;
  • sparse BM25 over the text;
  • graph mentions of the entities in the query;
  • recency, only for temporal questions.

It fuses the rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (k = 60; weights dense 1, sparse 1, graph 0.8, recency 0.5), splits the results into the context sections, and packs the most important items into a token budget (1200 by default). The rest is listed in ctx.omitted, and a session summary that does not fit whole is shortened. With intelligence on, a plan by intent sizes each section first.

ctx = memory.recall("How should I debug the OPC UA connection, and which vector store did we choose?",
                    user_id=user, session_id="s1", budget_tokens=800)
ctx.text            # the prompt-ready block
ctx.counts()        # items per section
ctx.omitted         # what the budget left out
memory.hybrid.search("OPC UA certificate", user_id=user, limit=5)      # the raw fused ranking, with signals

docs.title: Where the ideas come from
docs.text:
• Working, episodic, semantic and procedural memory follow the CoALA framework for language agents (Sumers et al. 2023, arXiv:2309.02427).
  • Episodic retrieval by recency, importance and relevance, and reflection: Generative Agents (Park et al. 2023, arXiv:2304.03442).
  • The working context, recursive summaries and archival memory: MemGPT (Packer et al. 2023, arXiv:2310.08560).
  • Strategies and lessons: Reflexion (Shinn et al. 2023, arXiv:2303.11366) and ExpeL (Zhao et al. 2023, arXiv:2308.10144).
  • Skills as a reusable, verified library: Voyager (Wang et al. 2023, arXiv:2305.16291).
  • The temporal knowledge graph with validity periods: Zep / Graphiti (Rasmussen et al. 2025, arXiv:2501.13956).
  • Memory updates: Mem0 (Chhikara et al. 2025, arXiv:2504.19413).
  • Linked, evolving notes: A-MEM (Xu et al. 2025, arXiv:2502.12110).
  • Plaintext, activation (KV) and parametric memory: MemOS (Li et al. 2025, arXiv:2505.22101).
  • Reciprocal Rank Fusion: Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher, SIGIR 2009.
  • Decision records: Michael Nygard, "Documenting Architecture Decisions" (2011).

The intelligence that manages these kinds has its own list in intelligence.md.

docs.title: Run it as a service
docs.text:
export KIOKO_API_KEY="$(python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))')"
kioko serve --db /data/memory.db --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8765 --intelligence

REST API            http://localhost:8765/v1   (OpenAPI: http://localhost:8765/v1/openapi.json)
MCP endpoint        http://localhost:8765/mcp

The agent loop is the same in every language: ask for memory before the LLM call, report the turn after it.

H='Authorization: Bearer '$KIOKO_API_KEY
curl -s localhost:8765/v1/recall -H "$H" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"user_id": "kumar", "session_id": "s1", "query": "Plan my weekend"}'     # -> {"text": "<memory>...", ...}
curl -s localhost:8765/v1/turns -H "$H" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"user_id": "kumar", "session_id": "s1", "user_message": "I moved to Pune", "assistant_message": "Noted!"}'
Endpoint Purpose POST /v1/recall · POST /v1/context Everything the agent should know for a query: a prompt-ready text plus every section (hybrid, planned, within budget_tokens) POST /v1/turns · POST /v1/learn After a reply: store the exchange and learn from it POST /v1/manage · POST /v1/plan · POST /v1/maintain · GET /v1/intelligence The intelligence: decisions for a turn (dry_run), recall plans, maintenance, status POST /v1/kinds/{kind}/{operation} · GET /v1/kinds · GET /v1/graph Every typed operation (goals/add, decisions/supersede, graph/neighbors ...), counts, the graph POST /v1/search · POST /v1/memories · GET · GET/PATCH/DELETE /v1/memories/{id} · DELETE /v1/memories?user_id= Search, create (through the write pipeline), list, read, edit, delete, clear one user GET /v1/pins · POST/DELETE /v1/memories/{id}/pin Pinned, always-at-hand memories GET/POST /v1/memories/{id}/links · DELETE .../links/{target} · GET .../links/{target}/explain · GET /v1/memories/{id}/related · GET /v1/graph/memories · POST /v1/graph/connect The memory graph: links, linking by hand, evidence, spreading activation, the graph for drawing, linking what was never linked POST /v1/messages · GET /v1/sessions · GET /v1/sessions/{id}/messages · POST .../summarize · POST .../end · DELETE /v1/sessions/{id} Sessions and short-term memory POST /v1/consolidate · GET /v1/cache · GET /v1/events?after=<seq> · GET /v1/users · GET /v1/stats · GET /v1/info Maintenance, caches, activity log, users, counts, configuration GET /v1/health · GET /v1/openapi.json Liveness and the OpenAPI 3.0 document (no key needed)

Import openapi.json (kioko openapi --server-url https://memory.example.com > openapi.json) into Postman, Swagger UI, Azure API Management or a Power Platform custom connector, or generate a typed client. Errors are JSON: {"error": "...", "code": "rejected"}, with 422 when a processor refused the content (for example a secret).

Security

Setting Behaviour API key KIOKO_API_KEY (or --api-key-env NAME). /v1 and /mcp then require Authorization: Bearer <key> or X-API-Key: <key>, compared in constant time. health and openapi.json stay open. Public bind Without a key, serve refuses any non-loopback address unless you pass --insecure. DNS rebinding Without a key, or with the console on, requests need an expected Host header (add names with --allowed-host). CSRF and Origin A request carrying an Origin header must be same-origin or from an allowed host. Origins listed with --cors-origin are also accepted, with CORS, on /v1 and /mcp only; the console never accepts cross-origin calls. --cors-origin '*' requires an API key. Request limits JSON bodies only, at most 1 MB, and a 30-second socket timeout.

One key grants access to every user's memories, which suits service-to-service calls. Put a gateway in front for per-user auth, and use HTTPS outside a private network.

docs.title: RemoteMemory and connect()
docs.text:
from kioko import connect, attach

memory = connect("http://memory-service:8765")   # RemoteMemory; API key from $KIOKO_API_KEY
memory.goals.add("Ship v1", user_id="kumar")      # every kind works remotely
memory.manage("We switched to pgvector", user_id="kumar", dry_run=True)    # so does the intelligence
agent = attach(my_agent, memory)                  # every adapter works remotely

RemoteMemory has the MemoryLayer API and return types (MemoryRecord, SearchResult, WriteResult, MemoryContext, ManageReport, RecallPlan ...). Rejected writes return None, a rejected update raises MemoryRejected, and an unknown id gives None / KeyError. Other failures raise RemoteMemoryError (.status, 0 when the service can't be reached). Idempotent requests are retried. Redirects are not followed, so the key never leaves for another host. subscribe() polls the activity log. Calls that act on memories need a user_id.

connect(target) accepts:

Target Gives you None $KIOKO_URL, else an in-process layer "memory://" an in-process layer "sqlite:///path.db", or a .db / .sqlite path a local SQLite layer "postgresql://..." a layer on Postgres + pgvector "qdrant://host:6333/collection" (qdrant+https:// for TLS) a layer on Qdrant "http(s)://..." RemoteMemory a .json path or a config dict MemoryLayer.from_config

kioko.intelligent(target, llm=None, ...) takes the same targets (except a service URL) and returns a self-managing layer. Anything with the same methods also satisfies the MemoryAPI protocol, so you can bridge another backend.

docs.title: Stores: where memories live
docs.text:
Every store holds every kind of memory, with the same behaviour. Pick one by URL:

Store connect() / kioko.intelligent() target Install Holds Good for In-process memory:// nothing memories, history, events (in RAM) tests, notebooks, demos SQLite sqlite:///memory.db or memory.db nothing (standard library) memories, history, events one machine, a service with moderate traffic Postgres + pgvector postgresql://user:password@host:5432/db pip install "kioko[pgvector]", or pip install "psycopg[binary]>=3.2" next to a wheel memories, history, events production: many processes, large memories, SQL operations Qdrant qdrant://host:6333/collection (qdrant+https:// for TLS) nothing (Kioko speaks Qdrant's REST API) memories (pair it with a history store) large vector workloads, an existing Qdrant cluster A Kioko service http(s)://memory-service:8765 nothing whatever the service uses sharing one memory across processes, languages and MCP hosts Your own MemoryLayer(MyStore()) — what you implement any database 
import kioko
from kioko import MemoryLayer

memory = kioko.connect("sqlite:///memory.db")
memory = kioko.connect("postgresql://kioko:<password>@db:5432/kioko")
memory = kioko.connect("qdrant://qdrant:6333/kioko_memories")
memory = kioko.intelligent("postgresql://kioko:<password>@db:5432/kioko")       # + self-management
memory = MemoryLayer.from_config({"store": {"type": "pgvector", "dsn": "postgresql://..."}})

kioko serve --store postgresql://kioko:<password>@db:5432/kioko --intelligence
kioko ui    --store qdrant://localhost:6333/kioko_memories

Keep passwords out of code and command lines that end up in logs. PgVectorStore() reads KIOKO_PG_DSN (or DATABASE_URL) when no DSN is given, QdrantStore() reads QDRANT_API_KEY, and describe() and the console show DSNs with the password redacted.

docs.title: Local databases with Docker
docs.text:
docker-compose.stores.yml starts Postgres with pgvector (pgvector/pgvector:0.8.7-pg17), Qdrant (qdrant/qdrant:v1.20.0) and a Kioko service on top of Postgres, with intelligence on:

export KIOKO_PG_PASSWORD='<choose one>'  KIOKO_API_KEY="$(python -c 'import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))')"
docker compose -f docker-compose.stores.yml up -d

export KIOKO_PG_DSN="postgresql://kioko:$KIOKO_PG_PASSWORD@localhost:5432/kioko"
export KIOKO_QDRANT_URL=http://localhost:6333
python examples/cookbook/17_stores.py          # the same code on SQLite, pgvector and Qdrant

The ports are bound to 127.0.0.1. For anything beyond a laptop, put the databases on a private network, set QDRANT_API_KEY, and keep passwords in a secret store.

docs.title: SQLite
docs.text: SQLiteStore(path, table_prefix="kioko_") keeps memories, session history and the event log in one file. It uses WAL mode and one serialized connection per process, which is fine for a service plus the console. Without a vector index, search scores every memory in the user's scope: a few milliseconds for hundreds of memories, about 150 ms for a thousand. Past that, use pgvector or Qdrant.

docs.title: Postgres + pgvector
docs.text:
from kioko.stores import PgVectorStore

store = PgVectorStore("postgresql://kioko:<password>@db:5432/kioko",   # or KIOKO_PG_DSN / DATABASE_URL
                      table_prefix="kioko_",       # several memories can share a database
                      ef_search=100,               # HNSW search breadth (pgvector's hnsw.ef_search)
                      iterative_scan="relaxed_order")
memory = MemoryLayer(store)          # history and events live in Postgres too

How it works:

  • <prefix>memories holds every memory. The embedding is a vector column plus its length (dims). Kioko creates an HNSW cosine index per embedding size, as a partial expression index ((embedding::vector(d)) vector_cosine_ops ... WHERE dims = d). Changing embedders therefore never breaks the index. Above 2,000 dimensions it indexes halfvec, which pgvector supports up to 4,000.
  • Filters on user, agent, session, kind and key run in SQL next to the vector search. With pgvector 0.8+, iterative index scans (hnsw.iterative_scan) keep filtered searches from returning too few rows.
  • <prefix>messages and <prefix>events hold session history and the activity log, which the console reads.
  • CREATE EXTENSION vector is attempted on first use. If your database user may not create extensions, an administrator runs it once.
  • Reuse your own connection with connection= (a psycopg 3 connection) or pool= (a psycopg_pool.ConnectionPool).

docs.title: Qdrant
docs.text:
from kioko import MemoryLayer, SQLiteStore
from kioko.stores import QdrantStore

store = QdrantStore("http://qdrant:6333", collection="kioko_memories", api_key=None)   # or QDRANT_API_KEY
memory = MemoryLayer(store, history_store=SQLiteStore("history.db"))
  • Every memory is a point. The embedding is the vector (cosine), and the fields are the payload. The point id is the memory id as a UUID, and the original id is kept in the payload.
  • Payload indexes on user, agent, session, kind, key and timestamps are created with the collection, so filtered vector searches stay fast. The collection is created on first use, once the embedding size is known.
  • Memories stored without an embedding (working memory) get a placeholder vector and has_vector=false, so vector searches never return them.
  • Qdrant holds memories only. Pass a history_store (SQLite or Postgres) for session history and the activity log. With connect("qdrant://...") they stay in process memory.
  • It needs Qdrant server 1.10 or newer (the Query API). There is no client library to install. The API key is sent as the api-key header and is never logged.

docs.title: Changing the embedder
docs.text:
After you switch embedders, for example from the offline HashingEmbedder to OpenAIEmbedder, run memory.reembed() once (per user with user_id=, if you prefer). It re-computes every vector that was made by another embedder and returns how many changed. SQLite and the in-process store would also re-embed old memories lazily the first time a search reads them. pgvector searches with its own index and only finds vectors of the current size: it creates the index for the new size by itself, but the old memories need reembed(). A Qdrant collection has one vector size, so use a new collection= per embedder.

Vectors do not record which embedder made them, so reembed() only notices a switch when the vector size changes. The offline embedder makes 1024-dimensional vectors, the same size as bge-large, mxbai-embed-large and e5-large. After switching to an embedder of the same size, run memory.reembed(force=True) to recompute every vector.

docs.title: Writing your own store
docs.text:
A store implements kioko.MemoryStore: insert, update, get, delete and query (filter + newest first + limit/offset). It can optionally implement:

  • vector_search(embedding, filter, limit), to let the database rank by similarity;
  • find_by_key, count, clear, touch and stats, which have defaults on the base class;
  • requires_dimensions / set_dimensions(n), if the database must know the vector size before the first write (as Qdrant does).

examples/04_custom_components.py has a JSON-file store in about 30 lines. Register it by name to use it from config and the CLI:

from kioko import MemoryStore, register

@register("store", "my-db")
class MyStore(MemoryStore):
    ...

or ship it as a plug-in with an entry point:

[project.entry-points."kioko.stores"]
my-db = "my_plugin.store:MyStore"

The contract tests in tests/test_layer.py (LayerContract) and tests/test_kinds.py (KindsContract) are reusable. Subclass them with a make() that builds a layer on your store, and every behaviour Kioko relies on is tested against it. The pgvector and Qdrant stores are tested exactly this way: offline against faithful fakes on every run, and against real servers in CI (KIOKO_TEST_PG_DSN, KIOKO_TEST_QDRANT_URL).

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text:
from kioko import WebhookSink

memory.subscribe(WebhookSink("https://hooks.example.com/memory", secret=os.environ["HOOK_SECRET"],
                             events=["memory.added", "memory.updated"]))   # prefixes like "memory." work too

Each event is POSTed as JSON from a background thread, so a slow or failing receiver never slows the agent. Each request carries X-Kioko-Event and X-Kioko-Delivery headers and, with a secret, X-Kioko-Signature: sha256=<HMAC>. Check the signature with kioko.sinks.verify_signature(secret, body, header). From the CLI: kioko serve --webhook URL --webhook-secret-env HOOK_SECRET.

docs.title: Fifteen kinds of memory
docs.text:
Kind Accessor Remembers Profile memory.profile who the user is: one value per slot, with history Factual memory.facts facts and preferences, with confidence and verification Semantic memory.semantic domain knowledge, shared by every user or personal; ingest() documents Episodic memory.episodes events with when, where, who and outcome; consolidated as they age Working memory.working(session) the current task's scratchpad: small, expiring, never embedded Conversational memory.conversation(session) rolling summary + recent turns, constant size Goal memory.goals objectives with priority, progress, due dates, sub-goals Procedural memory.procedures how-tos with versioned steps and a success record; standing rules Skill memory.skills reusable prompts, tools and code, ranked by relevance × reliability Strategy memory.strategies what worked for which kind of task, and what to avoid Decision memory.decisions decisions with options, rationale, outcome and supersession Graph memory.graph a temporal knowledge graph of entities and relations with history, and links between the memories themselves (serves, resolves, refines ...) KV cache memory.kv a byte-stable prompt prefix for provider caches; embedding and context caches Parametric memory.parametric the bridge to fine-tuned weights: export datasets, skip what a model has learned Hybrid memory.recall() dense + BM25 + graph + recency, fused with RRF, packed into a token budget

Details and APIs: memory types. Runnable recipes: cookbook.

docs.title: Every kind, on every surface
docs.text:
Each kind is reached the same way wherever your agent runs:

  • Python, in-process or remote. The accessors above, on a MemoryLayer or on connect("http://...") (RemoteMemory has the same API).
  • REST. POST /v1/kinds/{kind}/{operation}, with the method's arguments as JSON. GET /v1/kinds returns every kind's operations and counts.
  • MCP. Dedicated tools for goals, decisions, lessons and the graph; save_memory for facts, preferences, instructions, knowledge and episodes.
  • From conversation. With the intelligence on, manage(), record_turn(), POST /v1/manage, POST /v1/turns or MCP learn_from_conversation put each sentence into the right kind.

Whichever way a memory was written, it reaches the agent through recall() (REST POST /v1/recall, MCP get_memory_context).

All fifteen in one script (offline, no setup):

import kioko

memory = kioko.connect()            # in-process; connect("http://memory-service:8765") gives the same API remotely
user = "kumar"

memory.profile.set("location", "Pune", user_id=user)                                            # 1 profile
memory.facts.add("User's manager is Krutika", key="work.manager", user_id=user)                  # 2 factual
memory.semantic.add("OPC UA servers listen on TCP port 4840 by default", topic="iiot")           # 3 semantic (shared)
memory.episodes.record("Presented the maintenance demo", when="2026-10-20", user_id=user,         # 4 episodic
                       outcome="approved for a pilot")
memory.working("shift-1", user_id=user).set("ticket", "INC-4521")                                # 5 working
memory.conversation("shift-1", user_id=user).add_turn("The relay tripped", "Reset it at the panel")  # 6 conversational
goal = memory.goals.add("Ship Kioko 1.0", user_id=user, priority="high", due="2026-12-15")       # 7 goal
memory.procedures.add("Reset the safety relay", user_id=user,                                    # 8 procedural
                      steps=["Switch off the breaker", "Press reset for 5 seconds", "Switch it back on"])
memory.skills.add("summarize alarm log", description="Top recurring faults from a PLC alarm log",  # 9 skill
                  body="Summarize these alarms by fault code: {alarms}", user_id=user)
memory.strategies.reflect("debugging drives", "check the encoder cable first", "success", user_id=user)  # 10 strategy
memory.decisions.record("Vector store", chosen="pgvector", rationale="we already run Postgres",   # 11 decision
                        user_id=user)
memory.graph.add("Kumar", "reports_to", "Krutika", user_id=user)                                 # 12 graph
prefix = memory.kv.prefix(user_id=user)                                                          # 13 KV cache
rows = memory.parametric.export_dataset(user_id=user)                                           # 14 parametric
ctx = memory.recall("The relay tripped again, what do I do?", user_id=user, session_id="shift-1")  # 15 hybrid

print(ctx.text)

memory.graph.add("Kioko", "uses", "pgvector", user_id="kumar")          # the entity graph
memory.manage("We decided to use pgvector because we already run Postgres.", user_id="kumar")
# linked: decision "use pgvector because we already run Postgres" serves goal "Ship the Kioko memory layer ..."
#         (why: via Kioko uses pgvector)

memory.graph.links(memory_id)          # typed links with their evidence, weight and author
memory.graph.related(memory_id)        # spreading activation: what is connected, with the chain of links
memory.graph.explain(a, b)             # why two memories are, or are not, linked
ctx = memory.recall("line 3 is faulting with E-217 again", user_id="kumar")
# ... brings the fix that worked last time, and a "How these memories connect:" section

Each new memory is anchored (entities, rare words), compared with candidates from an inverted index, nearest neighbours and its session, scored with a noisy-OR of shared terms, meaning, entity-graph bridges and time, typed from the pair of kinds and cue words, and stored on both memories. Feedback ("that worked") adds resolves links and strengthens what was used; unused links fade. Graph memory has the algorithm, with formulas, worked examples and measured cost.
